Ordered list items stay on separate lines instead of being merged, including a list that starts on the line right after a paragraph without a blank line, a list that starts at 2 after a heading (rendered as items 2-5 with their real numbers, while a "3. " line inside a paragraph stays prose), and a fenced code block renders as a distinct block with its declared language label and a copy action that places its exact source on the pasteboard. A Markdown pipe table renders as a distinct bordered grid with a header row and data rows instead of raw pipe/dash text, preserving cell content and column alignment and wrapping a long cell onto every line it needs instead of cutting it off with an ellipsis, while CLI/XPC history preserves the exact raw table source text. Multiple plan deltas are summarized per item with count and byte totals at turn completion, with no per-delta notification records and no plan text in diagnostics. While the first plan is still streaming in and fits the viewport, the question that started it stays pinned near the top of the transcript, consistent with the user message preceding its final answer in CLI/XPC history. The plan streams in four held deltas that end inside a paragraph, inside a list item after it, and inside the fenced code block; CLI/XPC events carry exactly those deltas in order, and at each held stage the plan's one prose text view and its code block show exactly the text streamed so far, with nothing repeated or left over from an earlier stage, before the completed plan shows its whole code block.

A task with neither a repository nor a working folder can still plan, but once the plan exists its Start Implementing button is disabled and explains why: its tooltip and accessibility value read "Add a repository to this task to start implementing.", and a visible No repository warning beside it carries the same reason and opens the repository picker. Bridge state for the planned task has no workspace roots and no repository worktrees. Adding a repository gives the task a workspace root; in the still-open conversation the warning disappears and Start Implementing enables without reopening the task, then switches to Code mode and starts an implementation turn recorded after the plan turn, which runs in the task's created repository worktree as its only workspace root.

The composer keeps the committed model and effort stable while the picker is open, then updates when it is dismissed. Its popover lists provider models and includes an accessible discrete effort slider with Low, Medium, High, and Extra High choices, constrained by model-reported effort support when available; the visible opaque white knob has no focus border, the 6-point track is visibly thick, and the slider responds to dragging and keyboard arrows. A saved selection belongs to its conversation, persists through fresh CLI/XPC reads and reopening, and stays isolated between providers; legacy per-conversation selections remain available, while a provider-wide preference supplies the default for conversations without a selection. Effort persists per conversation. Malformed model IDs and unsupported efforts are rejected without replacing prior choices. The UI opens a second conversation, changes its model independently, and restores the first conversation's selection; unsupported modes and malformed model IDs are rejected before creating history.

CLI/XPC Goal set/get/pause/resume/clear persist the objective and lifecycle state across fresh connections and enable the Goals app-server feature; setting a first Goal on an Untitled task generates and persists its title from the objective before the Goal starts, while title failure uses the first eight objective words as fallback; setting the same active Goal preserves its timer generation, clearing then setting another Goal creates a new generation with a fresh baseline, setting a Goal moves the task to In Progress, and invalid blank objectives preserve the current Goal. The UI shows the generated title after reopening the task and restores saved Goals; the opt-in live Codex integration confirms native startup, verifies the first Goal retains its elapsed duration, restores a legacy completion without timing metadata, and confirms a second Goal timer begins near zero; renders each achieved summary as a conversation item that visibly moves with scrolling and is anchored to its completing turn, verifies a later user follow-up appears after the prior achievement through turn completion, and preserves both items and their ordering in the read-only Done archive. Native turn activation is owned by the retained GUI runtime.

A window and the CLI use one Codex app-server per Codex home. Every Codex request against one data folder (sends on two tasks, Goal set/get/pause/clear, history and usage refreshes, from the CLI and, in the UI, from an open window as well) runs on the same recorded server process, which listens on the shared unix socket with features.goals=true and the caller's CODEX_HOME and is the one live Codex manifest; it keeps running after every CLI Goal call, including a rejected blank objective, and a CLI call that spells the same CODEX_HOME differently reuses it. A send on the second task while the first task's Goal is active leaves that Goal active. The work turn Codex runs for the Goal is active and interruptible whether the window or the CLI set it; a history read, during it or after pausing the Goal ends it, and even with another model selected, never resumes the thread, because history is read from Playhouse's store. The Goal's work turn, which no send streamed, is recorded once from its streamed items when it ends and shows in history and the open window, without Playhouse ever reading Codex's thread. A usage read the server never answers times out without stopping the server and keeps the last known Codex account, and the next refresh reads it again. In the UI, the window sets a Goal and follows the turn Codex starts for it, which stays active and interruptible while the CLI sends on the second task and ends when the window pauses the Goal; a Goal the CLI sets appears in the open window without reopening the task, the window's pause and clear reach the CLI's Goal reads, and the Agents info block shows the Codex account read through that server.

A Codex app-server started under the earlier shared-client key, which also held two goal flags, is retired by the next daemon. When its daemon dies and a fresh daemon starts for the data folder, it reconnects to the legacy server only to retire it: with no turn left to follow, the server is stopped and its manifest removed, and the next Codex send, from the CLI or, in the UI, from the window, runs on one new server under the current key (executable, Codex home, data folder), leaving one live Codex server.
Claude AskUserQuestion requests with no questions are rejected through the control protocol, fail the turn, and mark the task Blocked; the UI shows the blocked task and its intervention indicator.

Claude's pending AskUserQuestion is persisted and restored from fresh CLI/XPC history after the provider turn ends; the task remains Waiting Response while unanswered, and answering resumes the saved Claude session in In Progress, delivers the answer, stores and shows the prompt that carried it as sent, clears pending state, and returns to Waiting Response. While the recovery turn applying the answer runs, the answered question is no longer pending in history or shown in the reopened conversation, which still shows the question that started it, and the task is In Progress; if that recovery dies mid-turn, the question returns for retry with the task in Waiting Response, and answering again succeeds.

A Claude AskUserQuestion asked during a Plan mode turn persists its mode; after its provider process ends, answering resumes the saved Claude session in Plan mode rather than silently downgrading to Code mode, relaunching the recovery turn with --permission-mode plan.

A Claude background Agent/Task call renders a live subagent activity that stays in progress through its launch confirmation and intermediate progress, resolves only once its real completion notification arrives, and keeps the turn open until then instead of settling early. A status-only completion update is not shown as an agent result; the summary-bearing notification is persisted as one normal assistant message in the parent conversation, appears in the visible transcript as the agent's row (named, finished working, with an arrow) rather than a reply bubble, opens the report in the read-only agent window when clicked, and survives fresh CLI/XPC history reads and app reopening without duplication. A failed background agent remains inspectable as a failed activity, and its error summary is not added as an assistant result. When a background agent's notification wakes the parent after its result, the turn stays open through that resumed work, including when the last agent finishes while the woken parent is still streaming, and ends only with the parent's next result, keeping its final answer and both agent reports. A failed agent whose notification the running turn already consumed ends the send promptly instead of waiting for a wake. The system prompt Playhouse appends for Claude lets it run shell commands and agents in the foreground or background, forbids only processes detached with & or nohup, says it can end its response while background work runs instead of waiting and must report the outcome only after the background results, and no longer tells it to sleep, keep shell commands in the foreground, or keep its turn open for work it started.

A Claude Bash call launched with run_in_background stays an in-progress activity after its launch confirmation and keeps the turn open after Claude's result while the shell runs, and still after the shell's notification empties the background task list, until the parent turn Claude Code wakes to deliver that notification sends its own result. The woken turn's answer is the final answer, the outcome it reports moves the task to Review without private outcome reminders, and the shell's completion resolves its activity with the command status without becoming an agent report. When the shell finishes before Claude's first result, so the woken turn starts before that result arrives, the turn waits for both results.

A Claude turn that reports completed and then leaves a background shell running, a dev server, settles in Review as soon as Claude's result arrives, without waiting for a notification that never comes and without a recovery prompt. A completed outcome reported while a background agent is still running does not settle the turn: the task stays In Progress while the agent runs, and when the woken parent turn then does more work and ends without a new report, the earlier outcome is treated as stale, so the task does not reach Review; Playhouse sends exactly one recovery prompt and the outcome reported in it places the task in Waiting Response. When Claude Code starts the woken turn for a finished background shell and then stays silent, with no outcome reported and no queued follow-up, Playhouse's backstop ends the wait and the same single recovery prompt decides the task's column instead of leaving it In Progress. The UI shows each task in the matching column and the recovery prompt in the transcript.

A Claude turn answers while a background review runs, the review's notification arrives right after that answer, and the woken turn adds nothing and reports no outcome; the review's report and the answer both stay in history, the answer once and as the final answer. Playhouse's private status nudge then starts a turn that keeps working, and a message the user steers into it is kept too: its commentary, its shell call, the background suite it launches, that suite's report delivered in a notification-driven woken turn, the screenshot it presents, and its final answer are streamed and recorded in order, and the completed outcome it reports moves the task to Review. Fresh history, a paged history read, and a later ordinary turn all keep that work, with the final report as the latest message before the later turn, while the nudge prompt Playhouse sent is shown once as its own message and no placeholder replaces it.

A Codex turn that reports no outcome receives Playhouse's private status nudge, and the nudged turn keeps working, with a message the user steers into it kept too: its commentary, its shell command, and its final answer are streamed and appear in fresh history after the earlier answer, with the shell command as a timeline tool row, and the completed outcome it reports moves the task to Review. Fresh history shows the nudge prompt Playhouse sent exactly once as its own message, with no placeholder replacing it; after a later ordinary turn the earlier nudge stays shown, the later turn's own nudge appears after its message, and no placeholder replaces either. The steered message is recorded inside the nudge turn it joined rather than as a turn of its own, and the transcript shows the turn's work above it and the final answer below it. The work the turn streams after the steer follows it, and while the turn still runs it renders below the steered message.

A Claude turn whose result is already out while a background shell keeps it open is still steerable: a queued follow-up's Steer reaches the running turn instead of silently staying queued, leaves the queue, appears in the conversation, and the turn waits for Claude's answer to it before the woken parent turn ends the send. The steered follow-up is recorded inside the turn it steered rather than as a turn of its own, so the transcript keeps it in order: while the turn runs and after it ends, the turn's work stays above its bubble, as does the answer given before it while it is shown, and what the turn said after it renders below it. Once Claude's answer to the steer has its own result while the shell still holds the turn open, that answer is already recorded in history exactly once, below the steered follow-up with the answer given before the steer above it, and stays shown rather than living only in the stream; after the turn ends both earlier answers are kept once as commentary and only the woken parent turn's answer is final.

A Claude turn that answers, then publishes a Playhouse progress report, which leaves that answer open, takes a steer at the report's tool boundary: the answer written before the steer is recorded once, above the steered message, as soon as the steer reaches Claude, rather than after Claude's reply to it, and the reply streams below the steer and stays shown while it is still being written instead of being cleared when the earlier answer is closed. After the turn ends the earlier answer stays above the steer as commentary and the reply is the final answer below it, each once. Only Claude Code keeps an answer open across a progress report, so Claude is the representative provider for this Playhouse-owned transcript order.

When Claude Code starts the provider turn that would deliver a finished background task's notification and then says nothing at all, Playhouse settles that turn on its own instead of leaving it open and the task In Progress forever: a follow-up queued while the turn was still parked stays queued through the silent wake, the send finishes and the task reaches Review, and that follow-up is then delivered in its own turn rather than stranded in the queue. A woken turn that is alive and merely slow to speak is not cut off by that backstop: it stays quiet past the grace a consumed notification gets and still ends the turn on its own answer.

If Claude fails while applying an answer after restart and echoes the answer or recovery instructions, Playhouse returns a generic error, preserves the pending question for retry while the task stays in Waiting Response, stores and shows the prompt that carried the answer as sent, and keeps it out of saved task state and diagnostics.

Codex's pending structured question persists after its provider process exits and leaves the task in Waiting Response while unanswered; Playhouse restores it from fresh CLI/XPC history, keeps provider switching blocked, requires the user to re-enter the secret once, and applies the answers in one recovery turn. The live recovery stream and the stored transcript carry the recovery prompt, assistant response, activities, and diffs exactly as sent, including the re-entered secret with its surrounding whitespace, and the visible UI shows them immediately and after app restart; saved task state stays free of the secret. A later Codex turn keeps its own diff and response visible in refreshed CLI/UI history alongside the earlier recovery response. In one task, a no-secret recovery response remains visible after a later secret recovery. The first prompt, delivered before the provider exited although its send reported failure, is in history, never returns to the composer, and is not saved as an unsent draft.

When Codex fails while applying recovered answers, Playhouse preserves the pending question while the task stays in Waiting Response, uses a generic visible error, stores and shows the sent recovery prompt as sent, and keeps the secret out of saved task state, diagnostics, and error text; later Codex thread read and resume failures do not affect history, which loads from Playhouse's own transcript store across fresh CLI/XPC reads and app restarts.

Claude AskUserQuestion requests are delivered through the control path and move the task to Waiting Response while pending; the question's Markdown, including a long paragraph, header, and option descriptions reach the client unchanged, and the UI renders the question inline with its Markdown formatted at the reply text size and its long paragraph wrapped in full across several lines without truncation, its header, and each option's description, preserves it across conversation switching, and sends a later answer to Claude before the turn ends in Waiting Response.

A successful Claude turn with an unanswered AskUserQuestion stays In Progress without outcome nudges; after the user answers, the next successful turn receives a hidden CLI status nudge. A question raised during that nudge is rejected through Claude's control protocol with completed, waiting-response, and keep-working instructions, which fails the private turn; the rejected question and the private rejection instructions stay out of the transcript, while a prompt that applied the user's answer is stored and shown as sent. Playhouse then stops driving the work and marks the task Blocked naming that reason.

MCP tool/requestUserInput structured questions raised in Plan mode remain in the conversation and move the task to Waiting Response while unanswered; leaving and reopening the conversation preserves the pending question, keyed answers resume the provider turn in In Progress, and the answered turn reports no outcome, so Playhouse drives a private status nudge; when that private turn cannot complete, the task settles in Blocked naming that reason instead of Waiting Response. A parallel conversation retains its own question and thread; the original conversation receives and answers a second question in its original Plan mode, and completing either conversation preserves the other pending request.

Non-blocking structured questions render inline, remain pending after switching to another conversation, and keep the task In Progress through fresh CLI/XPC history reconciliation after provider exit until answered. Free-text questions expose a selectable Other choice, select it when text is entered, keep it exclusive of listed answers, and deliver the free-text answer through CLI/XPC and visible UI. Answering resumes the provider turn without status nudges while its own pending question is still being resolved; the resumed turn returns to Waiting Response once the pending question clears, and the recovery prompt and response, including the secret answer, are stored and shown as sent.

Async agentMessage questions retain choices and a free-text prompt in live updates and fresh CLI/XPC history, retain accepted-turn model attribution during an active history reload, stay separate from later assistant text, and receive validated answers through the shared manager during and after an active turn. The UI shows inline answer cards instead of raw bullet text, blocks incomplete answers, preserves answered cards across reopening, and displays both submitted answers and responses.

An async question answered after its turn ends stays Pending when the first follow-up fails, rejects duplicate answers across fresh CLI/XPC connections, and becomes Answered only after an explicit queued retry succeeds. The paired UI keeps the card and queue action visible across reopening and then displays the delivered response. A fresh `conversation answered-async` read lists no answered questions while the answer is pending and lists the question once it is delivered. The failed answer is not kept in the conversation as a sent message, and the retry sends it exactly once.

Turn start persists In Progress; a genuine interrupted outcome remains Blocked with its reason, while restart recovery returns stale In Progress work to Waiting Response with its prompt and conversation available. A saved prompt whose turn never started returns to Waiting Response with its draft intact and can be continued; a turn running when the window quits cleanly or is killed keeps running in the bridge daemon, stays In Progress with its prompt visible after relaunch, finishes, and allows a follow-up. Interrupted outcomes and diagnostics persist across connections; a new prompt can finish in Review. The live turn's activity section renders open and folds away when the interrupted turn settles without an answer, on the conversation that stayed open; the interrupted turn adds no final answer and keeps the activity it reported. A queued follow-up remains visible as needing action after interruption, survives reopening, and is dispatched only after an explicit retry; the completed retry becomes the task's latest saved prompt. Recovering a never-started turn into Waiting Response starts Ping once.

A failed turn preserves its blocked reason and appears in the compact Blocked section above Backlog with a user-intervention indication; retrying clears that section, and the successful retry returns to Waiting Response without an explicit completed outcome.

The task view lists every file changed from the task branch's recorded base in a Changes section below a collapsed Viewed section, including committed branch changes and current staged, unstaged, and untracked edits, and excluding commits unique to the base branch. Marking a file viewed saves its current contents, stages the file in Git, and adds a Viewed entry that keeps showing the reviewed work from the branch base to that snapshot. Work done after that review is listed again under Changes and diffed against the saved snapshot, so one file can appear in both sections at once; a path with no content in the branch base and no current file is zero net change and is hidden entirely, even with a stale viewed snapshot, rather than showing a ghost entry. Selecting text or JSON files opens a calculated side-by-side diff whose header names the baseline used. Viewed snapshots persist across fresh CLI/XPC connections. Files that aren't current Changes entries, including already-viewed and unknown paths, are rejected by the mark-viewed CLI operation, and the UI offers that action only for Changes entries. Uncommitted filenames are green. Opening one diff after another serves each file's own content from the side-by-side editor the app loads once per session, so a later diff reuses that warm editor instead of starting Monaco again. Diagnostics record inventory and file-read outcomes without logging file contents.

The Changes section header offers Mark all as viewed while it lists files: one action saves a viewed snapshot of every current Changes entry and stages each in Git, so Changes empties and every file is listed under Viewed, and the operation reports how many files it marked, zero when nothing is pending. Each Viewed entry offers Mark as unviewed, which drops that file's snapshot without touching the Git index, so its whole change from the branch base is listed under Changes again; unviewing a file that isn't a current Viewed entry, including one already unviewed and an unknown path, is rejected. These results persist across fresh CLI/XPC connections. The Changes section collapses inside the task sidebar, hiding its Viewed and Changes lists while its header and pending count stay visible and the sidebar stays open for other sections; separately, the whole sidebar hides to a narrow rail that still shows how many files are pending. Each collapsed or expanded state is its own global preference, so opening another task keeps it. Once loaded, refreshing a task with no changes keeps its No changes state on screen instead of flashing the loading placeholder.

A newly created task branch with no branch or worktree changes starts with empty Viewed and Changes sections. External Git commits unique to the task branch and staged, unstaged, or untracked edits update the open task's Changes sidebar automatically; commits unique to the base branch are excluded. Fresh CLI connections report the same per-file inventory. When the base branch's local copy is stale behind its origin remote-tracking branch and the task branch has merged the newer upstream commits, those commits are excluded as well, so the inventory matches the pull request instead of the stale local branch. A local base branch that is ahead of its remote-tracking branch stays the base, so unpushed base commits merged into the task branch are not listed as task changes. While a merge is still open in the task's worktree, its files are held back and the sidebar shows a 'Merge in progress' notice naming the repository instead of the files the merge staged; the CLI reports the repository under mergingRepositories with empty sections, and aborting the merge lists the task's changes again.

A task whose worktree holds more than 1000 changed files still reports every one of them through fresh CLI connections, while the open task's Changes sidebar shows a 'Too many changes to list' notice naming the count instead of rendering the file list, so the window stays responsive. Bringing the count back under the limit lists the files again.

Each task's sidebar ends in a command row whose buttons sit at its right edge; it holds a terminal button. The terminal only ever opens in the task's created repository worktree, never in its source repository or a context folder, and never creates a worktree itself: while the task's worktree is still pending, or the task has no repository, the button is disabled and the CLI reports terminal_unavailable without creating the worktree, and the button enables in the open conversation once the worktree is created. The CLI reports how the terminal starts: the account's executable login shell with -l in that worktree, with TERM=xterm-256color and PLAYHOUSE_TASK_ID set, and the same answer on a fresh CLI/XPC connection; running that shell in that folder prints the worktree path and the task ID. Clicking the button slides a terminal panel in from the window's right edge, floating over the conversation's right side without moving or resizing the conversation, whose shell runs in the task's worktree with the task ID in its environment and which uses macOS Terminal's Clear Dark ANSI palette (such as its blue, distinct from the emulator's own default) on a solid black background, switching to the Clear Light profile's white background and blue when the app's appearance turns light and back when it returns to dark; hiding the panel keeps the same shell, so reopening it reaches the same process. Hovering the panel's left border shows the left-right resize cursor, and dragging it resizes the panel against the right edge, between a 320-point minimum and leaving 260 points of conversation uncovered, without resizing the conversation, and reopening the panel keeps the dragged width. Typing exit shows that the shell exited, and Restart starts a new shell, with a different process, in the same worktree. A task whose worktree no longer exists reports terminal_unavailable from the CLI, and the panel shows that error with a Try Again action that opens the shell once the worktree is back; an unknown task ID and the standalone chat's ID are not_found, and the standalone chat offers no terminal button.

A task with more than one created repository worktree opens its terminal as a split view with one shell per worktree. The CLI reports one pane per created worktree, in the task's repository order, each naming its source repository's folder and opening in that repository's worktree, never in a source repository, and the launch's directory is the first pane's; a single-repository task reports exactly one pane, and a worktree that no longer exists is left out while the others still open. In the app, opening the terminal for a two-repository task stacks one terminal pane per worktree in the panel, the first above the second, each headed by its repository's name and each shell running in its own worktree as a different process; hiding and reopening the panel keeps both shells. Exiting one pane's shell offers Restart only in that pane while the other shell keeps running, and Restart starts a new shell in that pane's worktree. A repository added to the task while its shells run gets its own pane when the panel is next opened, while the existing shells keep running.

The CLI confirms a new repository-backed task persists in Backlog; the UI shows no PR control there, then shows the active-card PR action after the conversation completes with a minimum 30-point hit target, on its own last row below the card title and time row and on the right, with that row absent while the task sits in Backlog. The active-card PR control visibly presents its native help on hover and keeps showing the pointing-hand cursor while its tooltip is up, with the arrow over the window's title bar, while hovering the card itself shows no tooltip and the card remains an openable control; the Done archive PR action remains available with its completed-task label and visibly presents its native help on hover with the pointing-hand cursor, then waits for the task lock before a real GitHub CLI or branch publication failure without saving a PR link or changing Done status. The card's PR button shows its full PR label with its hover capsule around it, not a truncated ellipsis; the button is the built-in pull requests plugin's, which `plugin list` reports as an enabled inline task card plugin.

A working-state task card (In Progress, Blocked, or Waiting Response) with no linked pull request shows the pull-request-mode plugin's compact mode pill in place of the manual PR button, closed on its current mode and defaulting to Manual; clicking it slides out Manual, PR, Green, and Merge, and choosing one selects it and folds the pill back onto it. The pill stays beside linked pull requests so autopilot and merge remain switchable. The mode is the plugin's own state keyed by task id, not a property of the task: a new task has no saved mode and is in Manual mode, choosing Manual clears the saved mode, every other choice (PR included) is saved and reflected across a fresh read, and a saved value no mode knows reads as Manual. When a turn completes in PR mode, the plugin creates the task's pull request on the way to Review with no user click, exactly once. Choosing Merge for that task in Review is a change the plugin acts on at once: it merges the green pull request with no other command, and the task stays in Review. In Manual mode, a new task's default, the task reaches Review with no pull request, and the existing manual PR button still creates it afterward unchanged. Every new task starts in Manual mode, whatever mode another task was left in. Creating a pull request with --if-needed for an unknown task is rejected. A task saved before the mode was the plugin's keeps its old Manual, Green, or Merge choice: the bridge imports it once into the plugin's state at its next request (a mode already chosen in the plugin wins, and PR imports nothing), and its card's pill shows it. In the same request, once, each task saved while PR was the default that still has no mode of its own gets PR saved as its own, so existing tasks keep opening their pull request on Review and their pill shows PR; a task created afterward still starts in Manual.

`task pr status` reports each linked PR's check state, failing check names, and a green, red, or pending health, and reads unresolved review threads only when asked (`--review-threads`, as every autopilot pass does), so a PR-mode card's probe never reads them; the board colours each linked PR number green, red, or blue by that health and keeps the mode pill beside linked PRs. `task pr autopilot` is one pass of the pull-request-mode plugin's Green mode, which the plugin runs for its Green tasks when they reach Review, when Green is chosen for a task in Review, and on focus; a pass leaves a task inactive unless it sits in Review with a linked pull request. With checks still running it sends no turn, and the plugin re-probes only those Green PRs on a slow poll until they settle. When checks fail or review threads are unresolved it sends one visible Playhouse autopilot fix turn through the task's provider that names the failing checks and unresolved threads, asks the model to judge every comment critically and to reply to and resolve each thread whether or not it changes code, and allows waiting-response for blockers it cannot fix (such as a GitHub outage or a Jira ticket the user must add); the task is In Progress during that turn and returns to Review when it reports completed. Once the PR is green autopilot sends nothing, never merges it, and resets its loop guard, so the same red state returning later (picked up by the focus probe) is fixed again. A fix turn that reports waiting-response stops the loop until the user sends the task back to Review, after which autopilot may try the red PR once more; a red state unchanged since the last fix moves the task to Waiting Response with a reason instead of being sent again, and the CLI case also drives the five-attempt cap to its Waiting Response stop after a fresh set of attempts (`--reset-attempts`, as choosing the mode again passes). A check rerun counts only by its latest run, as on GitHub: a failure followed by a newer success reads green with no failing checks, a success followed by a newer failure reads red naming the check, and same-named checks from different workflows stay separate (one failing workflow still reads red, failing names listed once), as do commit status contexts by context and untimed entries by rollup order. The pull-request-mode plugin's service runs these passes itself and records each follow: when Green is chosen for a task in Review, when a Green task reaches Review, on the slow poll while checks run, and on focus through its throttle (the CLI case counts three focus events within the cooldown as one follow at once and one when it ends); each pass records its result, and a pass skipped because the turn that moved the task to Review still holds it is looked at again on the poll. A pass the plugin started (`--confirm-with pull-request-mode`) asks it again right before merging or sending a fix turn, so a Green task's `--merge` pass merges nothing and reports inactive, and `--confirm-with` with no plugin id is invalid_argument. A shared status probe (`task pr status --shared`, as the card's plugins probe) shares a probe already running, so two at once ask GitHub once, and reuses its answer for a few seconds, while an explicit read always asks GitHub and leaves the shared answer alone; creating a task's pull requests or running a pass forgets the shared answer, and a failed probe is not kept.

Merge mode (a `task pr autopilot --merge` pass, which the pull-request-mode plugin runs for its Merge tasks) does everything autopilot does (it reads review threads, and red pull requests take the same autopilot fix path covered by the autopilot case) and also merges each linked pull request once it is green: with checks still running, or no checks reported yet on a freshly pushed head, it merges nothing and the task stays in Review; once checks pass (or the head has had no checks past the registration grace, as in a repository without CI) with no unresolved threads and GitHub reporting it mergeable, it merges the PR through GitHub CLI, pinned to the head commit it saw green, with the first merge method the repository allows (squash when allowed, otherwise a merge commit), exactly once; the PR reads as merged, the task stays in Review for the user to complete, and the card shows the merged completion action. A head that still has no checks after the registration grace is merged all the same. A merge GitHub refuses (for example a required review) moves the task to Waiting Response with GitHub's reason instead of retrying.

The real Git CLI detects merge conflicts without mutation, and PR creation still publishes the task branch and reaches the normal GitHub CLI path; conflicts do not block PR creation. CLI/XPC resolves staged conflicts locally without pushing and commits and pushes a staged resolution without changing the target. The paired UI confirms PR creation proceeds for a conflicted branch and the existing Fix Conflicts action still appears once the PR is linked.

A Review task whose linked pull request probe fails reports it: `task pr status` fails as operation_failed with the GitHub CLI's error, and the board raises its Pull request operation failed alert naming that error. Once the task moves to Done with --allow-unmerged, which removes its worktree, it is Done with no worktree left, a board probe that was already running when it moved raises no alert, and `task pr status` of the Done task lists only its recorded pull request, without probing, instead of the GitHub CLI's error.

Separate Review task cards probe their linked pull requests concurrently on app focus, with refreshes limited to one per 20 seconds, with focus events during cooldown coalesced into one trailing refresh. A conflicting PR or a mergeable PR whose remote head is not pushed locally retains the imported conflict action with its indicator artwork beside its PR link; the UI renders the artwork inside the action, keeps it beside the PR link, and gives both controls hit targets of at least 30×30 points. Clicking the conflict action sends the corrected request in the task conversation. CLI and UI use the same GitHub mergeability and head checks, retry once when resolution remains unconfirmed, and clear the action only after GitHub confirms the pushed head.

A completed turn outcome on a task with a PR-linked repository and a configured remote commits local work, merges new remote pull request commits, and pushes the branch before the task reaches Review, so the reviewed worktree holds no local-only changes. A linked repository without a publishing remote is left untouched and still reaches Review. When the sync cannot complete, the task moves to Blocked with the sync failure message instead of resting in Review, and a later successful sync pushes the stranded commits and returns the task to Review. While a provider turn holds the task's worktree, the sync command skips it untouched and reports turn-active. A worktree switched off its task branch fails the sync with a message naming both branches and blocks the task, leaving that other branch and the remote untouched; once switched back, a remote commit whose changes the branch already holds is concluded as a merge commit and pushed, the task returns to Review, and the next sync is up-to-date instead of failing on an unfinished merge. A merge Git refuses outright, such as one with unrelated history, blocks the task with Git's own error after the generic merge failure message, and restoring the remote branch heals it back to Review. A clean merge an earlier sync left unfinished on the task branch is concluded as a merge commit and pushed. A task branch deleted on a reachable remote is reported as no-remote-branch and leaves the task in Review.

When the remote pull request branch conflicts with local task commits, the review sync merges the remote branch and instructs the task's provider to resolve every conflict; if conflicts remain after the provider turn, the sync fails, the task moves to Blocked with the sync failure message, the merge stays in progress for manual resolution, and the remote branch is unchanged. A rerun with the conflicts staged commits the resolution, pushes the merged branch, and returns the task to Review. The board triggers the same sync automatically when a mergeable pull request's remote head diverges from the local head.

CLI/XPC creates PRs for two repositories, verifies the first PR persists when the second creation fails, retries only the missing repository, confirms each gh create call targets the corresponding repository worktree, and confirms both saved numbers on fresh reads. The UI labels active-card and Done-archive multi-repository creation actions PRs, clicks the active action, verifies the partial-success retry action, confirms the gh create calls target both repository worktrees and retry only the failed one, then shows exact PR numbers on the active task and Done archive, including four-digit values without grouping separators, each with a hit target at least 30 points wide and tall. Hovering the outer padded edge of each PR link triggers its feedback.

PR creation opens a pull request only for repositories whose task branch has commits its merge target lacks: in a two-repository task where only the primary worktree changed, gh create runs once, against the primary worktree, the primary saves its PR number on a fresh read, and the unchanged secondary keeps no PR link instead of failing the whole operation with GitHub's no-commits error and is remembered as skipped at its branch head, so the card offers no further create action; a review sync with no change keeps the skip, and once the primary's pull request merges and the task moves to Done, the Done archive shows the primary's PR link and no create action either. A two-repository task whose every repository is unchanged is rejected with a message saying no repository has changes to open a pull request for, with no gh create call and no PR link saved, and both repositories are remembered as skipped. After the task changes one of them, the review sync clears only that repository's skip, the card's create action counts it alone as a single PR, and creating it opens exactly one more pull request, for that repository. A later change to the still-skipped repository beside that linked PR brings back a single create action for the repository without a linked pull request, and creating it with a given --title and --body opens that repository's pull request with that title and body and links it too. The UI shows the primary's PR link after clicking the PRs action and reports the all-unchanged message in the failure alert.

Explicit app overrides reject obsolete compatibility metadata, foreign worktree or bridge identities, test IDs that do not match the current worktree, and nonisolated test data before launching; the current app preserves a saved draft across restart.
An invalid legacy database fails import without changing the source or publishing a destination or partial snapshot; the normal isolated board remains usable.

New tasks use the default provider from settings, which starts as Codex and rejects unknown providers, and task create can choose a provider explicitly and saves a --prompt description without starting the task, rejecting a blank or missing prompt; the UI shows that task in Backlog with the description unsent in its composer. A task without a conversation switches providers immediately; provider choice persists across fresh CLI/XPC reads and an app relaunch. Each provider's selected model becomes the default for conversations without an override; conversation-specific selections persist across provider switches and fresh CLI/XPC reads without reusing the other provider's model. Unknown providers and Done-task switches are rejected, and history has no provider boundary. A Claude task names Claude in the empty conversation, hides Goal mode, and rejects Goal changes through CLI/XPC. Switching a task's provider also updates the sticky default provider for new tasks and chats.

After a completed Codex fixture turn, switching providers is rejected while a follow-up is queued or a turn is active, and the provider menu is disabled during the turn. A settled switch to Claude records a boundary after the last Codex reply that persists across fresh reads and an app relaunch, keeps the Codex thread, and keeps earlier replies labeled Codex; switching back before any Claude turn removes the empty boundary, and the next Codex turn completes in the same thread.

Against the Claude Code protocol fixture, the answer Claude writes before running its Playhouse progress and outcome commands and the closing line it adds afterward form one final answer, not commentary, in the streamed final answer, fresh history, and transcript, and the reported outcome moves the task to Review. Text Claude writes before an ordinary tool stays commentary, and a turn that leaves every status nudge unanswered ends in Blocked. The fixture records the single private recovery prompt for each unreported turn; fresh history shows the nudge prompts and their replies. Switching to Codex hands off the whole Claude answer, excludes answered-turn commentary and private nudge prompts and replies including their redacted placeholders, and hands off only the last commentary from the turn that recorded no answer. A new Claude conversation with no explicit model pick dispatches to Sonnet and shows Sonnet as the picker default.

A standalone chat reports no task outcome, so it ends every turn with Playhouse's own chat page close-turn signal. When Claude runs that signal after its answer and before its closing line, the answer and closing line form one final answer, not commentary, in the streamed final answer, fresh CLI/XPC history, and the visible transcript, so the response is never left buried inside the collapsed Worked for disclosure; text written before an ordinary tool earlier in the same turn still stays commentary there, and the close-turn command really runs and succeeds. The chat instructions ask for close-turn before the final reply, which must end the turn, keep exactly one real close-turn per turn and no page bookkeeping in the answer, and carry no hidden escalation. A turn that runs close-turn first and answers after it shows exactly one final answer, filed onto the active page, with no nudge. When the turn ends on close-turn and Claude Code adds its own no-visible-output notice to the same turn, the notice streams once as a user-side message and stays in fresh history between the answer and what Claude writes after it, rendering as an automatic message from Claude Code rather than the user's bubble; that later text is a separate final message, so no bubble holds the answer twice, and the notice is never filed into a chat page. This classification is Claude-specific because Playhouse derives each message's phase from Claude's tool stream and only Claude Code adds such a notice inside a turn, while Codex reports the phase in its own protocol and never injects a hidden message into a turn.

When a standalone chat turn ends without its chat page close-turn signal, Playhouse sends exactly one follow-up turn through the same unsettled-turn recovery loop task conversations use. Its prompt starts with the Playhouse nudge marker, asks for close-turn on the previous reply and never for a task outcome, and stays in the chat transcript as an automatic message from Playhouse, followed by the agent's reply. A close-turn run in that nudge settles the turn and classifies the user's turn, which moves to the new titled page without the fallback classifier; the nudge turn and its reply are never filed into a chat page or replayed into a page's seeded context. A nudge that goes unanswered is not retried, the background classifier then decides the page, the chat never gets a board status such as Blocked, and task outcome is rejected for the chat. The nudge loop, the close-turn CLI and the turn outcome store are shared by Claude and Codex, so one representative provider (Claude) covers this case, and the round-trip case shows a Codex chat turn reaching the same nudge.

A standalone chat turn that is still running when its daemon dies is followed by the next daemon, and when it ends with close-turn --continues false that daemon files the turn's question and answers on the new titled page the close-turn opened, exactly once, leaving the earlier page as it was and no page decision pending. The page's first session is seeded with that turn, so the next question reaches the provider with the turn's question and answer. Filing reads Playhouse's own close-turn record and turn transcript, shared by Claude and Codex once a reattached turn ends, so one representative provider (Claude) covers this case.

A standalone chat turn that ran close-turn --continues false and then lost both its daemon and its agent before it was filed is filed, question included, by the next daemon on the page that close-turn opened, found from Playhouse's durable close-turn record. An answered turn that an earlier build left unfiled after its close-turn opened a new page, with no close-turn record, is filed by the next daemon as it starts onto the page opened while that turn ran. Both recoveries are recorded in diagnostics, a further daemon restart files nothing again, and the next question's fresh page session is seeded with the recovered turn. Recovery reads only Playhouse's own transcript, close-turn record and page store, so provider selection cannot change it; one representative provider (Claude) covers this case.

A Codex standalone chat turn survives daemon restarts, each of its agent messages stored on its own as the turn streamed it. A turn still running in its shared app-server when its daemon dies is followed by the next daemon, and when it ends with close-turn --continues false that daemon files its question and answers once on the new titled page, found from the turn's durable in-flight record and close-turn record, with no page decision left pending. A turn whose daemon and app-server both die after its close-turn opened a new page is filed on that page, with what its stored transcript holds, by the next daemon as it starts, before the next send seeds; that send's fresh page session carries the recovered turn, and the recovery is recorded in diagnostics.

A standalone chat turn that is still running when its daemon dies and then ends without close-turn is filed by the daemon that followed it on the active page, marked as a missed page signal, and handed to the background page classifier, which moves it to the new page it titles; the earlier page keeps only its own turn and nothing stays pending. When the daemon instead dies during the close-turn nudge that follows a turn without close-turn, the daemon that follows the nudge files the user's turn, never the nudge, hands it to the classifier the same way, and the chat keeps accepting sends. The missed-signal and classifier path is shared by Claude and Codex once a reattached turn ends, so one representative provider (Claude) covers this case.

The model picker removes the Default entry, superseded aliases, older versions, and duplicate snapshots, keeping only the newest concrete version in each family. GPT-6 Luna replaces GPT-5.6 Luna, and Claude Opus 5.5 replaces the Opus alias and older snapshots. Claude Code names its newest release only through an alias entry's resolved model, so that resolved version supersedes the older concrete Opus 5 and keeps Claude Code's own display name. Alias entries with no resolved model are omitted. A remembered selection the filtered list no longer offers moves to its family's newest offered model and is written back, surviving a later refresh whose list no longer offers that family, while a still-offered selection is left alone. A cached intermediate version advances again when live discovery returns a newer version, and the picker and persisted selection converge. A remembered bare alias migrates to its family's offered release, but a dated snapshot pinned through the CLI is left in place because its family's undated release is not a higher version. The shared CLI/XPC list applies the same filtering to Codex and Claude, and the visible picker matches the Codex list. The model popover opens above its composer control.

Playhouse stores each Codex message with the time it recorded it, and fresh CLI/XPC reads and app restarts show that same stored time. A timestamp in the provider's own thread history has no effect, because history is read only from Playhouse's store.

The selected effort persists through CLI/XPC reads and reaches Codex turn/start collaborationMode.settings.reasoningEffort; a model's advertised effort limit rejects unsupported requests before history is created. The UI selects Extra High and sends a Sol turn, then sends a Luna turn; each stored reply stays attributed to the model its own turn ran on, and both replies show their stored timestamps after an app reload.

After a Codex turn on a non-default model (Sol) ends, loading history never resumes the Codex thread, with Sol still selected or after the selection moves to another non-default model (Mini), and the stored reply stays attributed to Sol. A subsequent send on Luna also resumes despite Codex reporting Sol, starts the turn with Luna, shows its reply without an error, and records Luna for that turn. The selected model remains associated with the conversation. A second Codex conversation that never chose a model keeps the model its own turn ran on, in CLI/XPC reads and in the reopened composer’s picker, after the provider-wide remembered selection moves to another model.

Claude's model picker omits Default and aliases, showing Opus 5.5 resolved from Claude Code's bare alias entry as the concrete latest choice in place of the older Opus 5. Selecting it changes the prompt and reply label to Claude · Opus 5.5, and later model changes preserve the old reply's model attribution. The selected effort persists through CLI/XPC reads and reaches Claude Code as CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL; the UI selects Extra High and sends a Claude fixture turn whose recorded environment value is xhigh.

Codex and Claude filtered model lists persist across fresh CLI/XPC requests; an unavailable workspace fails refresh without clearing the previous cache. The visible Claude picker shows the seeded cached option before replacing it with the filtered versioned provider list, and retains an offline cached option when the provider executable is unavailable.

A misplaced pending question can be repaired through CLI/XPC only into its owning conversation. Repair rejects a wrong owner and a conflicting destination without mutation, applies both tasks' state atomically, preserves request identity and mode, clears only the misplaced source, and is retryable. Fresh history and the visible UI restore the question only on the original task; answering it clears pending state, and the recovery prompt and response are stored and shown as sent and survive reopening. Retrying an interrupted repair after the destination question was answered rejects the stale source without resurrecting the question.

The bridge daemon starts on the first request, exactly once even when callers race to start it, serves later requests from the same process, and stays alive while any connection (such as a window's runtime or CPU usage watcher) is open. A watcher receives the daemon's runtime snapshots as a turn starts and stops, and the daemon exits by itself once the last connection closes and no request is running; the next request starts a fresh daemon on demand without any manual step.

When the bridge daemon dies in the middle of a turn, that turn's send fails with a connection error instead of hanging, but the provider keeps running in its own session. The next request starts a fresh daemon on demand, which reattaches the running turn so the task stays In Progress with no restart notice, stops that reattached turn, and can then run and stop a new turn.

A Claude Code turn that writes its result while no daemon is running is finished by the next daemon from the run's log: the task leaves In Progress through the normal outcome path without a restart notice, and the result written during the downtime appears exactly once.

On a daemon's first request for a data folder, a process whose standard streams point into the folder's Claude or Codex run directories but that no run or server manifest accounts for is stopped, while a process writing into a run or server whose spawn is still being recorded is left alone.

`conversation watch` (conversation.events.subscribe) on a task with no running turn returns at once with watched=false, and fails for an unknown task. While a turn another caller sent is running, a watcher receives a `watching` event, the turn's live text deltas and its final `completed` history, while the sender still gets its own stream; the window streams such a turn the same way.

Stop works on a turn a fresh daemon reattached: for Codex it sends turn/interrupt over the reconnected socket and leaves the shared server running; for Claude it sends the interrupt with a request number past the old daemon's and then kills the run by its verified process identity and removes its folder. Either way the task settles in Waiting Response without a restart notice.

When a Codex app-server or a Claude Code run exits without finishing its turn while no daemon is connected, the next daemon settles the task as Waiting Response with 'The agent stopped while Playhouse was restarting. Your conversation is saved; send a follow-up to continue.', keeps the conversation up to the restart, and removes the dead agent's files.

A Claude Code turn with file-backed stdio keeps running when the daemon is killed: the next daemon replays the handled log without repeating its writes, keeps the task In Progress, shows the output written before the restart once, restores the still unanswered question and never answers an answered request again, ignores a late reply to the old daemon's request and numbers its own requests past the old ones, delivers a steered follow-up, streams the rest of the turn to a watcher, records the turn's usage once, settles it through its outcome, and removes the finished run.

A Codex turn keeps running in its shared socket app-server when the daemon is killed: the next daemon reconnects to the same server (no second server, one connection per daemon), keeps the task In Progress with no restart notice, shows the output written before the restart exactly once, saves the question the server re-sends on resume and answers the re-sent approval exactly once, accepts a steered follow-up, streams the rest of the turn to a watcher, and settles it through the normal outcome path. A turn that finished while no daemon was connected settles from the server's state, which the next daemon reads once to record the output it missed, exactly once and without an outcome command its answer echoed. A question the shared server raises on a thread no conversation owns gets no reply from the connected client, which leaves it for its owner instead of rejecting it.

A task starts with no recorded tokens, and its Token Stats modal says so plainly with no totals shown. Running a real Claude Code fixture turn parses that turn's reported usage into Playhouse's four buckets, adds them to the task's running totals, and records a per-turn row naming the provider and the tools, skills and MCP servers that ran in it. A second turn adds to the totals and appends its own row rather than replacing the first, and the per-tool rollup counts the turns each tool took part in. Call-level accounting spans the main agent and its subagents: an empty task's `callUsage` reports itself unavailable, and after a turn it reports exact model-call, total-sent, output and final-transcript figures read from the session files (counting each message ID once, ignoring repeated and zero-usage lines, and including the subagent's own file), which a second turn adds to rather than replaces. A Claude turn whose session files cannot be read still counts its calls live from the stream. The task card replaces its old dot with a compact live counter of total sent, which is hidden while that total is still zero, whose tooltip names the sent total, call count and final transcript size, and both the Token Stats context-menu item and a click on the counter itself, a button that highlights on hover, open a modal labelling 'Final transcript size' and 'Total sent (incl. subagents)' beside the call and output counts, the per-tool rollup and the per-turn breakdown. Excluding cache reads (uncached input + cache write + output, subagent included) is 855 per turn, doubling after a second turn, and also reaches the live stream when the session files cannot be read; an empty task reports it unavailable. A task saved before the cache split existed (call usage without the split, plus turn-level buckets) still loads, reports its call counts and total sent, omits the per-call excluding-cache figures, and falls back to the turn buckets minus cache reads (170 for 100 input, 50 output, 400 cache read and 20 cache write); its modal hides the Excluding cache reads headline. The modal also labels 'Excluding cache reads (incl. subagents)' with its main-agent and subagent split.

A Codex app-server fixture turn's usage reaches the same per-task totals and per-turn breakdown through Codex's own wire shape, mapping its cached-input bucket onto Playhouse's cache-read bucket and leaving cache-write at zero. The recorded turn row names Codex as its provider, Codex's input count includes its cached tokens, so the input bucket excludes them rather than counting them twice. Per-call usage notifications streamed before the turn ends, including those of a subagent thread that names its parent, reach the same call-level accounting once each (a repeated notification is ignored), and the Token Stats modal shows those Codex totals, call counts and final transcript size in the app. Excluding cache reads, the figure counts each call's uncached input plus cache write plus output, main thread and subagent alike (780), and the modal shows it with its main-agent and subagent split.

A task with no conversation reports its token map unavailable, with no wasters, tools or agents. After a Claude Code fixture turn whose session file logs every request (a shape, blobs, and transcript lines referenced by hash, including a parallel tool call sent as one message), the map reads the main agent and its subagent, and the main agent's final transcript tokens equal its last request's context exactly. The largest item is the MCP tool's 1,000-line log, ranked by the tokens it added, flagged as removed by the compaction, and sharing the tokens of the request it arrived in with its call by characters. The tools rollup ranks that MCP tool first by tokens added, the MCP server rollup counts its defined and called tools and what its definitions cost, the overhead lists the system prompt, each built-in tool definition and the server's definitions as sent with every request, the README read twice is one repeated result, the request that re-sent its context without the prompt cache is the one cache miss, and the compaction is counted. The Token Stats modal shows these in its Wasters, Tools & MCP and Overhead sections.

A Codex fixture turn whose thread and subagent have rollout files gives the same map from Codex's own format: a request was sent the instructions plus every item before its own output, the final transcript's tokens equal the last request's input exactly after a compaction replaced the history, Codex's unsaved tool definitions appear as one hidden-overhead item sent with every request, encrypted reasoning is shown by its size, the MCP tool's log is the largest item and was removed by the compaction, the repeated README read and the cache miss are reported, and the subagent's thread is its own agent. The raw input's final transcript lists the hidden overhead, the instructions and the replacement history once each without the removed log, and an item's full text, from a tool output or from the replacement history, reads back exactly as Codex saved it, in chunks, with its call named. The single-request scope rebuilds each Codex request from the rollout and labels it reconstructed: the latest request is the final transcript in order, request 4 flags both README reads and both of their outputs as exact duplicates, each request's items add up to the input Codex reported with its cached share as cache read and no cache write, and the JSON export holds the base instructions and the input items exactly as saved. The Token Stats modal shows the Codex wasters, the hidden overhead and the subagent, showing the log opens its full text, and the raw input's single request reads as reconstructed, with request 4's duplicates flagged.

A task with no conversation has no raw input: its page is empty and reading an item's text is not_found. After a Claude Code fixture turn, the raw input lists the final transcript with each item once across pages and without the log a compaction removed; the everything-sent scope adds what was removed, ordering by size lists the largest first, a search finds the log by a word only its full text contains, and a focus item reports its position. An item's full text reads back in chunks that end on a line break and join to the exact text, with the call that produced it named. An unknown agent or item is not_found, and an unknown order or a limit of zero is invalid_argument. In the app, View raw input opens the final transcript, scrolling loads the next page of rows, showing the largest waster opens it in the everything-sent scope with its full text, and scrolling that text reaches its last line.

After a Claude Code fixture session that resumes once its AGENTS.md changed, the raw input's single-request scope lists every item one request sent, in order and with nothing merged, and shows the latest request by default. A request after the resume carries both instruction copies in order, which differ and so are not flagged, while the date reminder sent twice word for word is flagged as a duplicate; a request before the resume carries one copy and no duplicates, and a search keeps each row's position. Each request reports Claude's input with its cache-read and cache-write split, and its items' sizes add up to that input. The request is labelled exact; its text export gives every item's full text under a header naming any duplicate, and its JSON export is the request body with the logged parameters, cache markers, system prompt, tools and messages verbatim, an earlier request's messages being a prefix of a later one's. A request number past the last is not_found, and zero or an unknown export format is invalid_argument. In the app, choosing Single request shows the latest request with its usage, both instruction copies unflagged and the repeated date reminder flagged, stepping back to a request before the resume shows one copy and no flags, Latest returns to the last request, and Copy all copies the whole request as JSON.

With a 150,000-token minimum, a Codex task reporting 900,000 context tokens runs its next same-model prompt without calling thread/compact/start or recording a compaction event, leaving the large context to Codex's native auto-compaction, and Playhouse passes no model_auto_compact_token_limit in its thread config. After a same-model turn records 220,000 context tokens, switching models compacts through the RPC first, records the old model and model-switch trigger, and waits for the matching successful terminal notification before turn/start. A failure after the initial acknowledgment is recorded as unsuccessful while the prompt still runs. If the app-server rejects compaction, Playhouse records a failed activity and event but continues the prompt. Codex uses reported context and model changes; its path does not depend on Claude's prompt-cache TTL or warm-idle scheduler.

Claude task launches never set CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW or any other value that shrinks or disables Claude Code's native auto-compaction, whether Playhouse's compaction triggers are on or off, and the settings no longer have a threshold: a threshold saved by an earlier build is ignored and settings load with their other values, the CLI rejects --threshold and saved settings stay unchanged. For an In Progress Claude task whose fixture session has 180,000 context tokens and has been idle 51 minutes, a scheduler tick runs one warm-idle /compact before the cache expires, records its trigger and before/after sizes in token usage, and a second tick does not compact again. Maintenance API token usage contributes to the task total. The conversation labels the maintenance activity as automatic without adding an empty assistant turn. Claude Code's own auto-compaction at its native window emits a provider auto-compaction boundary visible in the conversation and labelled Provider auto-compaction in Token Stats. The settings window shows and saves the enabled toggle, idle wait and minimum context with no threshold field, and its invalid-value alert leaves the saved value unchanged; negative and malformed integers are rejected without changing saved settings. Idle checks skip Done and Backlog tasks, contexts below the minimum, pending user-input requests, an active Claude turn, and an outstanding background task; eligible In Progress, Waiting Response, and Review tasks compact.

A Claude session with more than the minimum context is compacted before the next real prompt after its cache has been idle for over 60 minutes, and again before a model switch. The cold-resume and model-switch triggers are persisted with context sizes, each `/compact` fixture turn precedes the real prompt, the visible maintenance rows precede their corresponding prompts, and a model switch runs `/compact` with the old model before the requested model starts. When the cache is expired and automatic compaction is disabled, the first resumed response with near-zero cache reads and a large cache write records one cache miss, visible in Token Stats. If Claude reports a compaction failure, the failed maintenance row is recorded, the event is marked unsuccessful, and the user's prompt still runs and appears in history. Failed attempts are labelled as failures in the conversation and Token Stats. Stopping during compaction prevents the submitted work from starting.

The token usage color maximum defaults to twenty million, round-trips through the CLI/XPC settings commands, and rejects a non-positive value as invalid_argument without changing the stored setting. The settings window shows the stored maximum and saves an edited one, and a task card's token counter re-colors when the maximum changes so the same usage reads hotter against a smaller ceiling.

A newly created Claude task reports cpu-usage as not running before any turn starts. While a real Claude Code fixture turn burns CPU in a real child process, two successive `task cpu-usage` reads establish a baseline and then a plausible non-zero percentage for the task's process tree, the task card's CPU bar reads cool green against the default multi-core ceiling and hot red once the ceiling is lowered to match that load, and the reading returns to not-running once the turn completes.

Two Codex tasks rooted in different repository folders share one real fixture app-server. Before any turn each reports cpu-usage as not running. While task A's turn runs a real CPU-burning child process in A's folder and task B's concurrent turn runs an idle child in B's folder, both children belong to the same app-server process; once a baseline is sampled, `task cpu-usage` attributes a plausible non-zero percentage to A and a near-zero one to B, and the task cards show A's CPU bar reading hot against a lowered ceiling beside B's visible but empty bar. Both readings return to not-running once the turns complete.

The CPU usage color maximum defaults to one fully busy core per logical CPU, round-trips through the CLI/XPC settings commands, and rejects a non-positive value as invalid_argument without changing the stored setting.

Task status sounds are on by default and turn off and back on through the CLI/XPC settings commands, persisting across a fresh read; an unknown value is rejected as invalid_argument without changing the stored setting. With sounds off, a task that waits for a response and then settles in Review after its turn plays no sound and records the Ping and Glass it would have played as muted; once sounds are back on, the next such task plays Ping then Glass, and because the test runner sets PLAYHOUSE_MUTE_SOUNDS=1 each played sound is recorded as muted by the environment (played at volume 0). In the visible UI, the Workspace Settings Sounds toggle shows the stored setting and turning it off or on changes the setting the bridge reads.

The Agents info section reads Claude and Codex plan usage and accounts through the bridge. A refresh reads both providers: Codex's account, plan, both rolling windows (5h and weekly) with percent used and reset times, and its credits balance come from the app-server, while Claude's usage is read with Claude Code's get_usage control request, which has none for this account yet, so Claude starts with a signed-in account and no usage. While a usage watch remains open, it periodically refreshes both providers; Codex and Claude usage changed without a push reaches the watch and appears in the open window, and the Codex snapshot persists. A Claude turn's rate_limit_event then fills Claude's 5h and weekly windows and its warning status from the stream, a usage watch already open receives that change as a pushed update without asking again, a fresh read returns the same values, and the last-known snapshot is persisted to disk. A later event whose window reset time has already passed reads back as reset (empty, no reset time) and lifts the limit status without any provider call. Because Claude Code streams rate_limit_event only when a limit's status changes, and a usage-based plan's event has no utilization, every finished Claude turn reads the plan's usage again through get_usage (skipping the local transcript scan) without a refresh: the read replaces the windows with the plan's current ones, keeps get_usage percents as percents, shows a usage-based plan's monthly extra usage as a Spend limit row with the reset time from the stream's overage event, and is persisted; a refresh reads it too, a reply without plan usage keeps the last known rows, a reached spend limit reads as the limit reached, and a usage request that is never answered times out, keeping the last known rows, so later reads work again. Switching the Codex account signs out, clears the cached usage, starts a new login that returns its sign-in URL, and shows the new account's account and usage after the login completes; switching the Claude account does the same through the CLI and drops the old account's usage. A signed-out provider reports loggedIn false with no account or usage, a login restores it, and an unknown provider is rejected as invalid_argument. In the visible UI the Agents info section sits at the bottom of the left sidebar, below the Scheduled Tasks button and inside it, titled Agents info, with a separate compact Claude block and Codex block, each showing its account and plan together on the row beneath the provider name, its window rows with percentages and reset times, and a switch-account button; Codex's credits show in its block and Claude's warning status shows as Near limit. After a Claude turn whose usage read reports the plan's spend, the open window shows Claude's Spend limit row with its percent and reset time and the updated 5h row without a relaunch. A signed-out provider shows a Log in button instead of usage, which starts the login and brings usage back, and switching the account signs out and in without asking when no task for that provider is running. The section is open by default and its title is a button that minimizes it: the agent blocks go away and the title moves down to rest at the bottom of the sidebar, and expanding brings them back; the choice is remembered, so a section minimized before a relaunch is still minimized afterwards. Every read reports whether each CLI is installed from the same executable lookup Playhouse launches it with; an agent whose CLI is not installed has no block, and with neither installed the section is not shown. While a task for a provider is running, its switch-account button first asks for confirmation naming how many of its tasks are running, and cancelling keeps the account.

When a standalone chat's agent loads an earlier page into its context with `chat page read`, the conversation renders one deterministic "Recalling <page title>" line per loaded page, titled from the page archive rather than from anything the agent wrote, in the order the pages were read. The lines are visible in the turn that read them without opening the Worked for disclosure, stay once the turn settles and after a later turn and a reopen, and the read commands really run and succeed so the history carries each call and the page's own title. The line is derived from Playhouse's own provider-neutral command activity (a shell call titled "Running <command>" for both Claude and Codex) and the page store, so provider selection cannot change it; one representative provider (Claude) covers the shared path.

The Skills page opens from the Skills button beside the terminal button at the bottom of the task sidebar (the composer has no Skills button there; with the sidebar collapsed, its rail keeps that one Skills button and it opens the page) as a modal card centered over the task, a narrow column 403 points wide and nearly as tall as the window, over a dimmed backdrop, and its close button returns to the conversation. Opened from the composer's Skills button in a standalone chat, which has no task sidebar, its backdrop likewise covers the whole window rather than only the sidebar, the card centers in the window, and closing it keeps the chat open. It lists, in one sectioned list whose Repo, Global and Built-in anchors scroll it to their sections, the task's repository skills per repository (from each worktree's .agents/skills and .claude/skills, keyed by the source repository), the user's global skills (~/.agents/skills, Claude's skills folder, and Codex's legacy skills folder), and built-in skills (Codex's bundled .system skills, claude.ai-synced skills, and Claude Code's built-ins read from a provider session), whose section starts collapsed until its header or anchor expands it. The header shows the Skills | Rules | MCP tabs after the page's icon. Each section's header has an info icon whose hover hint (not a tooltip) opens below it and explains the section.
