Each skill row shows only its name led by one icon for the agents that can use it (the Claude logo for Claude only, the Codex logo for Codex only, a green check for both), on the name's line left of the name and without hovering, and its other details show in a hint left of the row while the pointer rests on it, which carries no provider icon: each user skill's row shows it usable by both Claude and Codex and its hint shows its description; a skill linked into both layouts is one Linked entry, two different skills with the same name in one repository are flagged right of the name as a conflict, a SKILL.md without valid frontmatter is flagged invalid and usable by neither provider, a repository without skills shows an empty state, and built-ins name only the provider they ship with. Reading a skill returns its SKILL.md, and an unknown skill is not_found.

Creating a skill writes SKILL.md with name and description frontmatter into the open Agent Skills layout, ~/.agents/skills for a global skill or the chosen task worktree's .agents/skills for a repository skill; invalid names, a missing description, a duplicate name, and the built-in scope are rejected with nothing written. Editing saves the new SKILL.md exactly as written, keeping frontmatter Playhouse does not parse, and rejects a renamed or description-less frontmatter while keeping the file. Clicking a skill row opens the editor modal straight on its whole SKILL.md, frontmatter included, with no structured header form, and its Preview tab shows that Markdown rendered with the frontmatter as a table; saving there writes the edited file, a description-less edit is rejected in the editor while keeping the file, and after the editor closes the page still answers clicks. A structured CLI edit rewrites the header (reading a YAML list as one field), removes an emptied field, keeps frontmatter Playhouse does not edit, and rejects an unknown field or an empty description while keeping the file. Clicking a built-in skill with a folder opens it read-only, without Save. New Skill asks only for a name, a description, and instructions it can preview, and a header field given to the CLI's create is written into the new SKILL.md. Moving a skill between a repository and the global gallery moves its folder and rejects a move onto an existing name. Deleting removes the folder from disk, built-in skills are read-only, and every change is visible to a fresh CLI process and on the Skills page.

Turning a skill off is stored by Playhouse rather than in either provider's settings, survives fresh CLI processes and reopening the Skills page, and can be turned back on. The row's actions menu has Disable, or Enable for a skill that is off, which takes effect as soon as it is chosen; a skill that is off shows grayed out, its menu's Use is disabled, and the row still responds, and turning a skill on disk on or off never starts a Claude Code session. Making a skill available outside Playhouse writes a real symlink into the other provider's layout (an absolute link in Claude's global skills folder, a relative link inside the repository), after which the skill shows as Linked; an existing file at the link path is left untouched and the request fails with already_exists, removing the outside link deletes only the symlink and keeps the skill, and a skill without a link cannot be unlinked.

Pressing and holding a skill row starts selecting skills, with no separate Select button: each editable row shows a checkbox that a click toggles, built-in skills show none and cannot be selected, and the header shows how many are selected with Fix, Delete, and Done. Deleting the selection after one confirmation removes every selected skill folder, repository and global alike, from disk, leaves unselected skills in place, forgets a deleted skill's off state, and ends selecting. A batch that includes a read-only or unknown skill deletes nothing and fails with invalid_argument or not_found.

A conflicting or invalid skill offers a Fix button on its row (and in the selection bar while selecting), and several selected skills can be fixed in one task. Fixing creates a task, on the source task's provider, whose saved prompt teaches the agent the skill format and lists each skill with its problem: repository skills by repository-relative path, to be fixed in the new task's own worktree of the source repository and committed and pushed like any code change, and global skills by absolute path, to be fixed in place with nothing to commit; the global skill folders are opened to the agent as context folders, and fixing only global skills needs no repository. The view switches to the new task's conversation, which sends that prompt as its own composer draft, leaving the composer empty and no unsent draft behind, so the turn runs in the new task's worktree with the global folders reachable. A skill with no problem, a built-in skill, an unknown skill, and a request without a task are rejected without opening a task.

A Claude turn sees the skills Claude Code does not read natively: Playhouse passes a Playhouse-owned --add-dir wrapper whose .claude/skills links to the task worktree's and the global .agents/skills folders, leaves skills Claude already reads out of the wrapper, and turns disabled skills off for that run with --settings skillOverrides, without writing to the repository or Claude's settings. Using a skill from the Skills page puts /skill-name at the start of the composer and the message reaches Claude Code unchanged. The resumed second turn gets the same wrapper, and turning the skill back on drops the override.

A Codex turn sees the skills Codex does not read natively: Playhouse gives the shared app-server extra skill roots made of Playhouse-owned wrapper folders that link to the task worktree's and the global .claude/skills folders, leaves the cwd repository's .agents/skills to Codex, and starts the thread with a per-thread skills config that disables both the task's disabled skills and other tasks' bridged skills, without writing Codex's config.toml. Using a skill from the Skills page puts /skill-name in the composer, and the turn sends Codex a structured skill input naming that skill's SKILL.md alongside the text; a later turn without a skill sends none.

A repository skill created with Private on is written only to Playhouse's private skill store, in a folder keyed by the source repository and laid out as .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md, with nothing written to the repository or the task worktree, whose git status stays clean. It is listed under its repository with scope private and a Private badge, every task on that repository sees it from its own worktree, and a task on another repository does not. A private skill cannot take a name that the committed skills of any of the task's repositories, the global skills, or the built-in skills already use, and a committed skill of the same name that appears later in a worktree takes precedence there: the private one is shown as Shadowed and used by neither provider. Editing saves the store's SKILL.md, a private skill cannot be linked outside Playhouse, Convert to Repository Skill moves it into the worktree's .agents/skills as a repository skill ready to commit, Make Private moves a repository skill back into the store and out of the worktree, Make Private to a repository moves a global skill into that repository's store, and Delete removes only its store folder.

A turn on a repository with private skills gets them as native skills, and a task on any other repository gets no extra folder, flag, or skill. Claude Code gets one more --add-dir, a Playhouse-owned wrapper named after the repository whose .claude/skills links to the store, so it lists the private skill and a /skill message reaches it unchanged; the link shows later edits, and a turned-off private skill is left out of the next turn without a skillOverrides entry and hidden from Codex threads. In a task with two repositories whose private skills share a name, each repository's wrapper is passed, and the later one is listed and invoked as /<repository>:<name>. Codex gets the repository's private wrapper among the shared app-server's extra skill roots, with other repositories' private skills disabled for its thread, and a /skill message, plain or namespaced, sends a structured skill input naming the private SKILL.md.

Typing @ in the composer opens a mention menu that lists, in order, the task's enabled skills, MCP servers, agents (Claude Code's .claude/agents and Codex's .codex/agents, an agent both define being one item that names both files, the running provider's first), repositories (the task's own and those under the repository root), then the other tasks on the board, never Done ones, and never rule files; before anything was mentioned, an empty query shows that whole list, grouped under a header per kind. Typing after the @ filters it, items whose handle starts with the query first, and a query nothing matches shows an empty state. The arrow keys move the highlight, Return or Tab inserts the highlighted item, and a click inserts the clicked one, as @handle drawn in the accent color; Escape closes the menu while keeping the typed text. Sending appends a <playhouse-mentions> block naming each mentioned item with its full path or details (for the task's repository, also its worktree), only for known handles that start a word, and the provider receives it while the transcript shows only the typed message, once, with its mentions drawn in the accent color, and the task's saved prompt keeps the typed text. Steering an active Codex turn expands its mentions the same way, exactly once, and shows the steer once, while a steer that misses its turn is queued as typed. The sent mentions become the recent mentions, most recent first and ten at most, which an empty query then shows instead, and they persist across fresh CLI processes. A task moved to Done leaves the list, its query matches and the recent mentions, and a mention of it is sent as typed. Listing mentions without a task is a usage error, and for an unknown task is not_found.

The Skills page, titled Skills, Rules & MCP, switches to its Rules list with a Skills | Rules | MCP picker. Rules lists, in one sectioned list whose Repo, Global and Managed anchors scroll it to their sections, each task repository's instruction files from its worktree (AGENTS.override.md, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .claude/CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md, and every .md file under .claude/rules, keyed by the source repository and the file's path), the user's global rules (~/.agents/AGENTS.md, Codex's AGENTS.md, and Claude's CLAUDE.md and rules folder), and the organization's managed CLAUDE.md. Each rule row shows only its name led by one icon for the agents that follow it (the Claude logo for Claude only, the Codex logo for Codex only, a green check for both), without hovering, and its other details show in a hint while the pointer rests on it, which carries no provider icon: each rule names the agents that follow it in Playhouse sessions and the ones that read it natively: a repository AGENTS.md beside a CLAUDE.md is followed by both but read natively only by Codex, ~/.agents/AGENTS.md is read natively by neither yet shared with both, a CLAUDE.md symlinked to AGENTS.md is one Linked rule read natively by both, AGENTS.override.md is Codex's own and leaves the AGENTS.md beside it to Claude, a .claude/rules file shows its paths globs, the managed CLAUDE.md is Claude's only and read-only, and an @import of a missing file is flagged as a problem. A repository without rules shows an empty state. Reading a rule returns its file exactly, and an unknown rule is not_found.

New Rule writes the shared AGENTS.md (the chosen task worktree's, or ~/.agents/AGENTS.md for a global rule) or, given a name, a topic file in .claude/rules (the worktree's, or Claude's global rules folder) whose paths frontmatter lists the globs given; empty instructions, an invalid name, globs without a name, the managed scope, and an existing file are rejected with nothing written, and the source checkout is left alone. Clicking a rule opens its editor on the whole file with a Markdown preview, and saving writes the file exactly as typed; empty instructions and a rules-folder file whose frontmatter never closes are rejected while keeping the file. The managed CLAUDE.md opens read-only without Save and can be neither edited nor deleted. Deleting a rule removes its file from disk, and every change is visible to a fresh CLI process and on the page.

A lone AGENTS.md that both CLIs already read on their own shows Both CLIs rather than Linked, since nothing links to it. Turning a rule off is stored by Playhouse rather than in either provider's settings, survives fresh CLI processes and reopening the page, and can be turned back on; the managed CLAUDE.md can't be turned off. A turned-off rule Codex reads itself, such as the working repository's AGENTS.md, still lists Codex and the page says Codex still reads it, while a rule only Playhouse shares, such as ~/.agents/AGENTS.md, reaches neither agent. Making ~/.agents/AGENTS.md available outside Playhouse writes absolute symlinks as Codex's AGENTS.md and Claude's CLAUDE.md, after which it is one Linked rule read natively by both; a repository CLAUDE.md gets a relative AGENTS.md symlink beside it. An existing file at a link path is left untouched and the request fails with already_exists without writing any link, a rule Codex has no place for can't be linked, and removing the outside link deletes only the symlinks.

A rule with a problem offers a Fix button on its row, which creates a task on the source task's provider whose saved prompt explains how both agents read rules and lists each rule with its problem: repository rules by repository-relative path, to be fixed in the new task's own worktree and committed and pushed, and global rules by absolute path, to be fixed in place with their folder opened as a context folder, and fixing only global rules needs no repository. The view switches to the new task's conversation, which sends that prompt once and leaves no unsent draft. A rule with no problem, the managed rule, an unknown rule, and a request without a task are rejected without opening a task.

A Claude turn follows the rules Claude Code does not read itself: after the task instructions, its appended system prompt carries ~/.agents/AGENTS.md with its @import of another file expanded inline, Codex's global AGENTS.md, and the AGENTS.md of the task's other repository, plus a pointer naming the globs and file of that repository's path-scoped rule; rules Claude reads itself, such as Claude's global CLAUDE.md and the working repository's CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md, are not repeated. Because the working repository has both AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md, --settings tells Claude Code to read both, and a rule turned off on the page is excluded for that run with claudeMdExcludes, without writing to the repository or Claude's settings. The resumed second turn carries the same rules, and turning the rule back on drops the exclusion.

A Codex turn follows the rules Codex does not read itself: after the task instructions, the thread starts with developer instructions carrying ~/.agents/AGENTS.md, Claude's global CLAUDE.md, and the working repository's CLAUDE.md and always-on .claude/rules files, with CLAUDE.md's @AGENTS.md import left out because Codex already reads that file, and each path-scoped rule as a pointer naming its globs and file rather than its text. The working repository's AGENTS.md and Codex's global AGENTS.md are not repeated, a rule turned off on the page is left out, and Codex's config.toml is not written. A thread resumed on a fresh app-server gets the same rules.

The Skills page, titled Skills, Rules & MCP, switches to its MCP list with a Skills | Rules | MCP picker. MCP lists, in one sectioned list whose Repo, Global and Managed anchors scroll it to their sections, each task repository's servers from its worktree's .mcp.json and .codex/config.toml (keyed by the source repository and the server's name), the user's global servers from Claude Code's ~/.claude.json and Codex's config.toml, and the organization's managed-mcp.json. Each server row shows only its name led by one icon for the agents that start it in Playhouse sessions (the Claude logo for Claude only, the Codex logo for Codex only, a green check for both), without hovering, and its other details show in a hint left of the row while the pointer rests on it, which carries no provider icon: each server shows its command or URL and only the names of its environment variables and headers, never their values, and names the agents that start it on their own and the ones Playhouse passes it to: a .mcp.json server is Claude's own and passed to Codex, a server defined the same way in both global files is one entry both CLIs start, a server only one CLI defines is passed to the other, an SSE server or one with a working folder reaches only the agent that can run it with the reason shown, a server Codex's config.toml turns off reaches neither, a server written inline in config.toml is listed but not editable, two global definitions that differ are flagged as a conflict, and the managed server is Claude's only and read-only. A repository without servers shows an empty state and an unreadable configuration file is reported. Reading a server returns its full definition, and an unknown server is not_found.

New Server writes a global server straight into both Claude Code's ~/.claude.json mcpServers and Codex's config.toml [mcp_servers] table, with ${NAME} environment references written as Codex env_vars and every other setting, comment and server in both files kept; a repository server goes into the chosen task worktree's .mcp.json and the source checkout is left alone. An invalid name, a missing command, an SSE server, a URL that is not http, an environment reference Codex can't pass through, the managed scope, and an existing name are rejected with nothing written. Clicking a server opens its editor, and saving rewrites it in every file that defines it while keeping each provider's own keys, such as Codex's startup_timeout_sec and Claude's oauth; an invalid edit and an edit to a server written inline in config.toml are rejected while keeping the files. Deleting a server removes it from every file that defines it, and every change is visible to a fresh CLI process and on the page. Right after a create closes its panel, one click on New Server opens it again.

Turning a server off is stored by Playhouse rather than in either provider's configuration, survives fresh CLI processes and reopening the page, and can be turned back on; the managed server can't be turned off. A turned-off server in Claude Code's own configuration still lists Claude and the page says Claude still starts it, so turning it off applies to Codex only, while a turned-off server only Codex defines reaches neither agent. Make Available Outside Playhouse writes a Claude-only global server into Codex's config.toml, a Codex-only one into Claude Code's ~/.claude.json, and a repository .mcp.json server into the worktree's .codex/config.toml, after which each is one entry both CLIs start; a conflicting server can't be linked and nothing is written.

A server whose definitions conflict offers a Fix button on its row, which creates a task on the source task's provider whose saved prompt explains how both agents configure MCP servers and lists each server with its problem: repository servers by repository-relative file, to be fixed in the new task's own worktree and committed and pushed, and global servers by absolute file path, to be fixed in place with their folders opened as context folders. The view switches to the new task's conversation, which sends that prompt once and leaves no unsent draft. A server with no problem, a managed server, an unknown server, and a request without a task are rejected without opening a task.

A Claude turn starts the servers Claude Code does not read itself: its --mcp-config carries Codex's own global servers (with env_vars passed as ${NAME}), the working repository's .codex/config.toml servers, and the other task repository's .mcp.json servers, but not the servers Claude Code already reads or ones turned off on the page. Its --settings starts the working repository's .mcp.json servers that are on with enabledMcpjsonServers and skips turned-off ones with disabledMcpjsonServers, without writing to the repository or either provider's configuration. The resumed second turn carries the same servers, and turning a server back on adds it.

A Codex turn starts the servers Codex does not read itself: the thread's mcp_servers config carries the working repository's .mcp.json servers and Claude Code's own global servers, translated so ${NAME} environment references become env_vars and an Authorization bearer token becomes bearer_token_env_var, leaves out an SSE server Codex can't run and the servers Codex already reads, and turns off a server Codex may read itself (from its config.toml or the working repository's .codex/config.toml) that is turned off on the page with enabled = false, without writing Codex's config.toml. Turning servers on or off on the page resumes the thread on its next turn with the new mcp_servers config.

Opening the MCP page asks both agents on its own, with no button to press, which servers they start and which need a sign-in, showing Checking sign-in… while they answer and asking again whenever the page is opened: Claude Code, asked with the task's own MCP bridge, reports each server including the ones Playhouse passes it, and Codex reports its own; a server that needs a sign-in shows a Sign in badge with the Claude or Codex logo on its row (labelled Sign in for Claude or Sign in for Codex), and the claude.ai connectors and plugin servers Claude Code starts that no file defines are listed under Also started by Claude Code in the Managed section, a connector that needs a sign-in with the same badge. Asking for one provider only asks that provider. An agent that can't be asked is reported by name on the page while the other agent's answer is still shown.

The Sign in badge with the Claude or Codex logo on a server (labelled Sign in for Claude or Sign in for Codex) is the button that signs in: it asks that agent to start the OAuth sign-in of that one server (Claude Code's mcp_authenticate, Codex's mcpServer/oauth/login) and returns the authorization link, which the page opens in the browser (a test build only records it, and never opens one) while the badge reads Waiting… (labelled Waiting for sign-in…). A server both agents have shows one Sign in button per agent on the same row, each just that agent's logo so the name keeps room in the narrow card (labelled the same way): each starts only its own agent's sign-in, waiting on one leaves the other clickable, and each badge clears on its own once that agent is signed in. The agent finishes the sign-in when the browser redirects back to it, and the page then checks again by itself and the badge goes away; waiting for it through the CLI keeps the bridge running and returns signed in. Starting one agent's sign-in never asks the other agent, a sign-in nobody finishes times out with a message that names the server, and waiting for a sign-in that was never started or was already reported with either agent, an unknown provider, and a blank server name are rejected or reported without starting anything.

The Plugins menu opens the Plugin Catalog, whose sidebar lists every atom (Stack, Text, Icon, Image, Label, Button, Link, Spinner, Spacer, PillPicker, Card, Disclosure, Panel, Meter, Scroll, Divider, ChoiceBar, Toggle, TextField, Segmented, Menu, PressArea, Overlay, Editor, Popover, StepSlider, Modal, Page, SidePanel) and the Task Item, Agents Info, Token Stats, Skills Page, Repository Chips, Composer and Done Archive examples; each atom page renders its JavaScript page through the React renderer into native SwiftUI with no plugin error and lists the atom's props. Clicking a Button atom runs its JavaScript onPress handler, whose state change commits a single text op on that Text's string node, and clicking a Disclosure's title runs its onToggle handler, which collapses it (its children hide while staying in the tree: one commit updating only the Disclosure's props and the state readout) and expands it again, and clicking a ChoiceBar's option runs its onChange handler with that option's value, which selects it (one commit updating only the ChoiceBar's props and the readout), while clicking the option already selected commits nothing, and the Scroll page's scroll view shrinks to its four rows, then, once added rows pass its 120-point maxHeight, stays 120 points tall and scrolls to reach the last row. On the Skills page's controls' pages, clicking the Toggle runs its onToggle handler, which flips it (one commit updating only the Toggle's props and the readout), typing in the TextField runs onChange with the new text, Return in it runs onSubmit and an arrow key runs onArrow with its direction, choosing a Segmented segment runs onChange with its value, choosing a Menu item runs onMenu with that item's id, and the PressArea tells a click (onPress) from a press and hold (onLongPress). On the Overlay page, the badge drawn over the chip's top trailing corner leaves the chip its own size and runs its own onPress. `plugin render` runs a plugin headlessly through the same runtime and node tree: the first render is one commit, each event sent by testID runs its handler and commits only the ops for the nodes that changed (a toggled label is one text op on one node), an interval advanced with --advance updates only its own node, and every bundled catalog page renders without errors. An unknown atom, an unknown or mistyped prop, a missing required prop, an event the atom doesn't raise, a child the atom can't hold, a string outside a Text, or a handler that throws is reported in errors with exit 1 (a mistyped or missing prop, decoded straight from the plugin's values, names its path and what is wrong, such as size: expected a number, found a string or options.0.label: missing), and an event for a missing testID, an event the atom has no handler for, or an unknown catalog page is refused as invalid_argument. Commits, the plugin's props and event values cross between JavaScript and Swift as JavaScript values with JSON.stringify's rules: props keep their types and nesting, NaN becomes null, a Date becomes its ISO string, undefined, function and inherited fields are left out of nested values, toJSON is called once per value (one that returns itself gives an empty object), an event value arrives as a string, and a circular prop or an op whose node id is out of range is reported in errors. The Button page also shows a link-style Button and a large one (taller than a regular Button), each running onPress, the Menu page's disabled Run Now item is shown but can't be chosen, and the Icon page draws the app logo asset in its own colors (original) in a 50-point frame with its accessibility label; a mistyped original or Menu item disabled is reported with its path. The Scroll page's lazy paged list raises onEndReached each time its end scrolls into view: it starts at 1 pages loaded, and scrolling to its end appends a page and then, scrolled to the new end, another (2, then 3 pages loaded); in `plugin render` each onEndReached is one commit that adds the page's rows and changes the readout. The TextField page's plain field (style plain) draws no border on its rounded Stack, so it is shorter than the rounded field, and typing in it runs its onChange.

The Plugin Catalog's Stack page draws a surface on a Stack in both axes, while its Stacks without surface props draw nothing: a column filled accent at 0.18 with an accent border and an 8-point radius keeps its children at its top leading corner, inside its padding, when its 220-point minWidth and 90-point minHeight are larger than they are; a capsule row filled #2E7D32 with a dashed border lays its icon and text out side by side on that green; and a border-only Stack with align unset (a Stack's default, center) and fillWidth stretches across the page, draws its border and no fill with rounded corners, and keeps its text centered both ways in its 60-point minHeight. Blocking the JavaScript item changes only its status message and the toggle's label (one commit: text, update, text on three nodes) while the native item keeps its own state, clicking the JavaScript card runs its onPress handler (Opened 1 times, one text op) without re-rendering the title or the card, and right-clicking the JavaScript card offers the native card's menu, whose Move to Done runs onMenu with its id (Last: menu done). The Plugin Catalog's Agents Info page shows the Agents info section composed in JavaScript from atoms beside the native SwiftUI section the board uses, built from the same atoms and sample data: both show the Agents info title button (Expanded), a Claude block above a Codex block with the same account and plan rows, window rows (label, percent, usage bar and reset time), Codex's credits, its Near limit status and the updated hints, each at the same size in both, and the JavaScript tree uses only atoms (Disclosure, Panel, Meter, Stack, Text, Icon, Button, Spacer) with the board section's identifiers. The Plugin Catalog's Kanban Column page shows the board's columns composed in JavaScript from atoms beside the native SwiftUI columns the board uses, built from the same atoms and sample models (a column's cards are native and not part of the page): each side shows a Backlog column with its Add button and its empty state, an In Progress column with a count of 2 and no empty state, a Blocked column with the Waiting for user intervention notice and its empty state, a Waiting Response column washed in its purple accent (a tint Panel filling the column with a soft fill and hairline border in the accent, its pixels visibly purple beside the other columns, and its count in the accent) and its empty state, and a Done column with its empty state, with the board's identifiers (column-heading, column-count, add-backlog-task-button, empty-state, blocked-waiting-indicator), and every one is the same size in both and reads the same text (the uppercased title, the count, No tasks yet with Create a task to get started or Drop a task here). Pressing the JavaScript Add button runs its onPress in JavaScript (Last: add) as one commit that changes only the readout, and the native Add button runs its own handler without touching the JavaScript side. Plugins present UI the three ways the board does, each a controlled atom whose first child is what it is presented from and stays laid out as usual. On the Plugin Catalog's Modal page, the Open modal button runs onPress (Last: open) and opens a 320-point sheet over the window that starts with the standard header its title props describe (its icon, the Modal title and its subtitle, and a close button) above content that brings no padding of its own yet sits 24 points in from the sheet's edges (the default inset) and a default spacing below the header, with a Done button; Done closes it (Last: done), the header's close button closes it through onDismiss (Last: dismiss), and Escape closes it again through onDismiss. On the Popover page the anchor opens a popover whose content, again with no padding of its own, is inset 14 points by default and spaced apart, and Escape dismisses it; a titled Modal and a second Popover each override inset to 0 and spacing to 4, which the UI geometry and `plugin render` tree both confirm. On the Page page, Open page (Last: open) slides a page over the whole 420 by 220 point view below it, covering that view's frame and showing its title, and its Back button closes it (Last: back), uncovering the view. On the SidePanel page, Open trailing (Last: open trailing) slides a 200-point panel as tall as the 480 by 240 point view below it in over that view's trailing edge, Open leading (Last: open leading) over its leading edge, and the panel's close button closes it (Last: close). `plugin render` keeps each atom's presented content in the tree after its first child, and opening or closing is one commit that updates only the presentation atom's props and the readout. `plugin render` reports the Modal's title, subtitle and icon with no inset or spacing set and the Popover's content with no Stack of its own, and an explicit inset and spacing override the defaults with no errors. Only a Modal raises onDismiss: a Page or SidePanel given an onDismiss handler, or a Modal, Page or SidePanel without isPresented or with a mistyped width or edge, or a mistyped Modal title or inset or Popover spacing, is reported in errors.

The Plugin Catalog's Done Archive page shows the board's Done archive composed in JavaScript from atoms above the native SwiftUI archive the board presents, built from the same atoms and sample model, each opened by the board header's archive button (the bordered Button atom with the archivebox icon, labelled Done tasks) into a 340-point SidePanel over the trailing edge of a 560 by 460 point stand-in for the board, open at first. Both show the Done tasks title and its close button, the search field with its Search tasks and conversations placeholder, and a list of five rows, each a button opening its task with the done checkmark, its title and its date, beside its pull request actions: a #227 link valued merged (its PR's state, which also ends its help), a PR button beside a #228 link, a PRs button, a disabled busy PR button showing a spinner, and nothing for a task without repositories, each at the same size in both and with the board archive's identifiers (done-archive-task, done-archive-create-pr, done-archive-pr-link, done-archive-search, and done-archive-list valued 5 tasks loaded). The JavaScript tree uses only atoms (SidePanel, Stack, Text, Icon, Button, Link, Spinner, Spacer, Divider, TextField, Scroll), its search a plain TextField on a rounded Stack. The list's end is in view, so its onEndReached runs on both sides (End reached). Typing in the JavaScript search runs onChange (Last: search followed by the text), narrows the rows to the matching title and shows the clear button, which clears the search and brings every row back; a search that matches nothing shows No matching tasks instead of the list. A PR button runs its handler with its task (Last: create pr followed by the title), a row runs open (Last: open followed by the title) and slides the panel away, the archive button opens it again (Last: toggle open), and the close button closes it (Last: close), while the native archive keeps its own state. The list raises no onPress, so pressing it is refused as invalid_argument.

The Plugin Catalog's Token Stats page shows the Token Stats modal composed in JavaScript from atoms above the native SwiftUI modal the board presents, built from the same atoms and sample data, each opened by the task item's token counter (the same overhanging Button atom, labelled with its description and hinted Open Token Stats). Choosing Wasters in the JavaScript section bar runs onChange with its value (Last: section wasters) and shows the largest items, each with a 72-point share bar, its kind, the removed-by-compaction flag, its request count and a small Show button, then the repeated result and the cache miss, while the native modal stays on Overview until its own bar moves it, after which both show the same rows at the same size. Tools & MCP lists each tool's bar, calls and total and the MCP server, and Overhead lists what every request carries and each agent. The overview scrolls within at most 320 points and each map section within a fixed 420. Done closes the JavaScript modal (Last: done) and leaves the native one open, and the counter opens it again (Last: open). The section bar raises no onPress, so pressing it is refused as invalid_argument.

The Plugin Catalog's Skills Page shows the Skills modal's header and skill list composed in JavaScript from atoms above the native SwiftUI header and list the Skills modal uses, built from the same atoms and sample data, each 403 points wide like the modal and opened by the Skills button (the same plain Button atom with the sparkles icon, labelled Skills). Clicking the JavaScript Built-in header runs its handler (Last: expand builtin) and shows its skills. Pressing the JavaScript Global anchor runs its handler (Last: jump global) and asks the list to scroll to Global (scrollTo global, a new scrollRequest on each press) while every section stays in the list, and an anchor expands a collapsed section. The menu's Use runs its handler (Last: use release-notes) without re-rendering any row, and its Disable runs onMenu (Last: toggle release-notes off), which grays the row out, disables Use and offers Enable, while the grayed-out row still responds to clicks; Enable turns it back on (Last: toggle release-notes on). Clicking a skill's text runs onPress (Last: open release-notes); pressing and holding it runs onLongPress, which starts selecting (Last: select release-notes): its row shows a checked checkbox and the accent highlight, the rows' own controls hide, built-in skills show no checkbox, and the search's row shows 1 selected with Fix, Delete and Done; a click on another row adds it (2 selected), and Done ends selecting (Last: done selecting). The actions menu runs onMenu with the chosen item's id (Last: menu release-notes edit), typing in the search runs onChange with the text, choosing Rules hides the anchors and the search, and the close button closes the JavaScript modal (Last: back) while the native one stays open, until the Skills button opens it again (Last: open). The search field raises no onPress, so pressing it is refused as invalid_argument.

The Plugin Catalog's Repository Chips page shows the task header's repository chips and the Add repository picker their + button opens, composed in JavaScript from atoms beside the native SwiftUI chips and picker the task header uses, built from the same atoms and sample models. Typing in the JavaScript search runs onChange (Last: search pla); Down and Up run onArrow (Last: down, then Last: up) and move the highlight while the native picker's highlight stays put; Return runs onSubmit with the highlighted row (Last: submit mobile-app) and closes the picker; the + button shows it again (Last: open picker) and hides it (Last: close picker); clicking a row runs its onPress (Last: select Website); Change… runs its handler (Last: choose folder); clicking a chip runs its onPress (Last: edit backend) without re-rendering the other chip; and its remove badge removes it (Last: remove backend) while the native chips keep theirs. A chip for one of several worktrees of a repository (Playhouse on second-line) shows its branch in 11-point secondary text after the name, at the same size in both, and its actions name that worktree: clicking it runs Last: edit Playhouse-second-line and its remove badge removes just it (Last: remove Playhouse-second-line). The Plugin Catalog's Composer page shows the conversation composer's box composed in JavaScript from atoms above the native SwiftUI box the conversation uses, built from the same atoms and sample data, each as wide as the page's 764-point column and with the composer's identifiers (the native side prefixed native-), and the JavaScript tree uses only atoms (Panel, Stack, Editor, Button, Icon, Menu, Spacer, Popover, Text, Divider, StepSlider). Both show the editor with its message placeholder, the attach button (a Button labelled Attach files with the paperclip icon), the Skills button (the plain Button atom with the sparkles icon, labelled Skills), the Plan button (labelled Plan mode, the lightbulb.max icon) and the Goal button (labelled Goal, the GoalIcon asset), both Off with no highlight, the Claude provider menu, the Sonnet 5.5 model button with its Medium effort, the schedule button and a send button that is disabled while the draft is empty, each at the same size in both. Typing in the JavaScript editor runs onChange (Last: edit) and enables Send, Send runs its handler (Last: send followed by the draft) and clears the editor, and the native editor keeps its own text. The attach button runs onPress (Last: attach). The Plan button runs onPress (Last: plan on), reads On with an orange highlight and icon and shows the Start Implementing button, and pressing it again turns Plan off (Last: plan off) and hides Start Implementing; the Goal button (Last: goal on) reads On with an orange highlight and shows the goal placeholder, and turning Plan on turns Goal off and turning Goal on turns Plan off, so the two are never on together; choosing Codex in the provider menu runs onMenu (Last: provider codex) and shows its title.
