The schedule button opens its popover (Last: schedule open), whose content stays native. The conversation's own composer is this box: with Debug ▸ Highlight Native Atoms on, a task's composer shows its editor as an Editor atom, its model button in a Popover atom and its provider menu as a Menu atom, with its attach, Skills, Plan, provider, model and send identifiers. A Popover shows the children after its first (its anchor) in the popover, so one with only an anchor is valid.

Add Plugin mode is off by default; the Plugins menu's Add Plugin Mode item and `plugin mode --on` turn it on, `plugin mode` reports the saved state to a fresh CLI process, `--off` turns it off, and any other option is refused as invalid_argument. While it is on, a bar across the top of the window explains the mode and its Close button turns it off; the board's sidebar shows a labeled Add here button below Scheduled Tasks and each task card's bottom row shows an Add here icon, which Close removes; an open task shows its sidebar expanded even when the sidebar was collapsed, with a labeled Add here button as the sidebar's first section, above Changes, an Add here icon before the sidebar's Skills and Terminal buttons and an Add here icon at the start of the composer's toolbar, which has no Skills button in a task; and the standalone chat shows only the composer's Add here icon. Turning the mode off from the CLI removes every placeholder live and returns the sidebar to its saved collapsed state.

Plugin edits persist as an isolated draft, saving publishes a new version and preserves history, discard restores the saved preview, and restoring an older version publishes it as a new revision. A draft with no unpublished changes can't be published: `plugin save` refuses it as invalid_argument and adds no version, and `plugin versions` reports `hasChanges`. In the editor, Publish is disabled and Discard changes is hidden until the draft differs from the published plugin, and both return to that state after publishing or discarding.

A plugin that was never saved is discarded entirely: `plugin discard --id` on a new authoring session, before any prompt and after a turn wrote its draft, removes its draft folder and its editor conversation, so `plugin sessions` no longer lists it, `plugin edit --id` is not_found, and the plugins revision is bumped; `plugin delete --id` removes an unsaved plugin the same way. Discarding or deleting an unknown id is not_found, a saved plugin's discard still only resets its draft and keeps its editor, and when its draft can't be removed an unsaved plugin keeps its editor conversation for a retry. In the window, the Plugins menu lists each unsaved plugin as its own submenu labeled with its name, placement and (Unsaved), offering Edit and Delete, with no Edit item at the menu's root. Discard changes in an unsaved plugin's editor, shown even before it has a draft, asks to discard the plugin, then closes the editor and removes the plugin from the menu; Delete in its submenu, after confirming, removes another one the same way.

Plugin authoring starts with centered name and presentation setup, then opens a standalone conversation beside a live preview with an empty composer, guidance to describe the plugin, the chosen name, placement and presentation with a note that the user can ask to change any of them, no repository title, no provider turn, and no board card or task header. The editor header shows “Plugin editor” beside its back button. The user can choose a model and write an unsent description; the Plugins menu reopens the same conversation and preview with its draft and history. Name, presentation, placement and generated plugin identity persist in provider instructions, which let the user change any of those choices, even the name; a changed name, placement and presentation names the unsaved draft's editor and is published under the same plugin ID on save; invalid setup is rejected. Claude and Codex receive the setup and bundled skill without installing files in the user’s home.

A Codex plugin editor sends the user’s description with the chosen name, presentation, placement, generated plugin identity and permission to change any of those choices in thread instructions, points it at the CLI's plugin-editor help for its commands, automatically supplies the bundled plugin skill, and restores the same setup when the thread resumes on a fresh app-server. The composer starts empty and no turn starts until the user sends.

A plugin editor follows a running Claude turn after a daemon restart, restores its answer once alongside the preview, and settles without a task outcome nudge. Claude represents the shared reattachment settlement used by both providers.

Edit on a plugin whose editor conversation has a turn running opens that conversation at once: while the editor's Claude turn has streamed its first answer and still holds its turn, the editor that sent it shows the turn running, `conversation runtime` lists the editor's task ID in activeTaskIDs (and drops it once the turn ends), and `plugin edit --id` returns within seconds with the same editor ID and the turn keeps running, and in the window the plugin submenu's Edit…, from the board and again with the editor already open, shows the editor with its preview and the running turn's pause button without closing it, and the output the turn streams next appears live in the reopened editor, as it does for `conversation watch` on the editor. Once the turn finishes its reply follows in the same conversation; `plugin sessions` lists the editor, `plugin discard --id` resets the saved plugin's draft and keeps its editor, and deleting the plugin removes its editor from `plugin sessions`. Opening an editor is Playhouse-owned and provider neutral, so Claude represents both providers.

`plugin list` reports the built-in Changes plugin first (builtIn, valid and enabled, at the conversation sidebar with the inline presentation), then the task card's built-in Pull request mode and Pull requests plugins (inline at the taskItem placement), the board sidebar's built-in Agents info (a section at the mainSidebarBottom placement) and its built-in Scheduled Tasks (a popover at the mainSidebar placement), and the composer's built-in Built-in Commands (headless at the composerActions placement, with its / commands), before the installed plugins. A built-in can't be deleted, edited or rendered headlessly (invalid_argument), and an installed folder with a built-in's id is invalid. An inline plugin is valid only at the conversation sidebar or on the task card. `plugin disable --id` and `plugin enable --id` work on built-in and installed plugins, bump the plugins revision and persist across fresh CLI reads. A `plugin refresh` with nothing changed still bumps the revision and lists identical plugins, and in the window it leaves an open plugin submenu open. A disabled plugin is listed with enabled false, is not run when plugins are refreshed, and `plugin render` refuses it as unavailable until it is enabled again. An unknown id is not_found, a malformed or missing one invalid_argument, and a deleted plugin installed again starts enabled with no saved state. An inline conversation sidebar plugin receives `workspace` (its revision and the open diff) and `sidebar` (whether it is on the rail) props, and its Playhouse.ui.refreshWorkspace and openDiff calls are recorded headlessly, while the board's sidebar refuses them as unavailable. In the window, the Plugins menu has a Built-in Plugins section whose Changes submenu offers Disable but no Edit or Delete, and which labels Built-in Commands Headless (slash commands only), its submenu also offering Disable but no Edit or Delete. Disabling Changes removes the task sidebar's Changes section and labels it Disabled, and enabling it brings the section back. An installed plugin's submenu offers Disable beside Edit and Delete, and disabling it removes its button until it is enabled again. An installed inline plugin renders in place in the task sidebar with no entry button: its refreshWorkspace raises the workspace revision, its openDiff opens the window's diff view for a real change and the open diff reaches its props, and on the hidden sidebar's rail it reads that it is on the rail. Each plugin keeps its own saved values: `plugin state --id` reads them and `plugin state --id --key --value <json>` stores one (null removes it) and bumps the plugins revision; `plugin list` reports each plugin's `state`, which an installed plugin gets as `props.state` and stores with Playhouse.setState (recorded headlessly), and the built-in Changes keeps its state the same way. An unknown id is not_found, and an empty key, a missing value or a value that is not JSON is invalid_argument without bumping the revision. A fresh daemon reads the disabled ids and saved states back from settings, and authoring an inline plugin outside the conversation sidebar or the task card is invalid_argument. In the window, the inline plugin's Playhouse.setState comes back as its props.state, and collapsing the Changes section saves its collapsed state as its plugin state. After a relaunch a disabled Changes stays hidden and labeled Disabled while the plugin keeps its saved state, and enabled again, Changes comes back collapsed. An open page plugin receives its newly saved state, and disabling a plugin closes its open surface.

Each plugin is a folder in the data directory's plugins folder holding plugin.json (id, name, icon, placement, presentation) and its script. `plugin list` reports only the built-in plugins at first; after plugins are written, `plugin refresh` validates every folder, bumps the plugins revision, and reports the valid plugin beside invalid ones with their errors (an unknown placement or presentation, a manifest id that does not match its folder, a missing manifest or script, and a script that throws or uses an unknown atom when rendered once with sample context), which a fresh `plugin list` reports the same way without bumping the revision. The CLI reports each plugin's name, icon, placement, validity and first validation errors, and deleting through `plugin delete --id` removes only that plugin's folder. In the window, each plugin has its own submenu labeled with its placement, containing Edit, Delete and a disabled Settings placeholder; an invalid plugin's first error is inside its submenu. The Plugins menu visibly lists each plugin with a submenu indicator and opens a submenu with Edit, Delete and disabled Settings actions; an invalid plugin's first error is visible in its submenu. After a refresh the window shows the valid plugin's button at its placement. Deleting a plugin from its submenu after confirming, or with `plugin delete --id`, removes its folder, its button and its menu entry; an unknown id is not_found and an id that is not a plugin folder name is invalid_argument.

An installed plugin receives its placement's context in Playhouse.props: the plugin and the appearance everywhere, the task with its repositories and context folders in the conversation placements, and the composer's draft and selected text in the composer placement, while the board's sidebar gets no task. `plugin render --plugin <id> --task <id>` renders it headlessly with that real context. Playhouse.bridge runs any bridge command but plugin render against the real store (a rename is seen by a fresh CLI process) and rejects a failing one with its code; Playhouse.ui close, openTask and the composer's setDraft, insertText, replaceSelection and focus are recorded headlessly; a composer call from the board's sidebar and a plugin render call are refused the same way in both hosts; and --task without --plugin or an unknown plugin is refused. In the window a page plugin from the board's sidebar covers the board, reads the real board, and its openTask opens that task without sending anything, keeping the page open behind it, so going back from the task returns to the page; a composer popover plugin opens anchored to its button showing the draft and the selected text, and its replaceSelection replaces the selected text in the composer; a sidebar plugin from the conversation sidebar slides in at the trailing edge showing the task's title and repository, inserts text after the selection, replaces the draft, renames the task, and closes with its close button; and a modal plugin beside the Terminal button opens as a sheet with the task's context and closes itself with Playhouse.ui.close. Every presentation starts with the app's standard modal header (the plugin's icon, its name and a close button) above the plugin's atoms, which bring no padding of their own yet sit inside the presentation's inset, as does the header: 24 points in a page or sheet, 20 in a sidebar, and 16 in a popover, whose header title is smaller than a sheet's.

Plugins have a fetch(url, options) global that makes HTTP and HTTPS requests from every placement, answered by the same core in the window and in `plugin render`; the cases reach a local fixture server instead of the internet. A fetch on mount shows the server's greeting; a GET resolves with its status, a response header read case-insensitively and a JSON body; a POST sends its method, headers and text body, which the server receives; a 404 resolves with ok false and its text body; a redirect is followed and reported as redirected with the final URL, while a URL with no path is not; a refused connection rejects with network_error; and a non-http URL such as file:// rejects with invalid_argument without any request. `plugin render` records each fetch in hostCalls as net.fetch with its arguments and result, and `plugin refresh` keeps a plugin that fetches on mount valid. In the window a page plugin from the board's sidebar shows the fetched greeting and each button's result.

An Image atom shows a picture its window loads natively from its url. An installed page plugin's circular 48-point Image of a PNG served over http from 127.0.0.1 draws the picture's red and blue halves clipped to a circle and is one accessibility element with its label, a 64 by 32 file:// Image draws the same PNG from the plugin's folder with its corners rounded, an unlabeled Image of the same URL is decorative (hidden from accessibility), and an Image whose URL answers with something that isn't a picture, or whose server refuses the connection, draws its placeholder symbol instead, with no plugin error. The window loads the served picture once: the copies mounted together share one request, and a second copy mounted by a re-render (the readout reads Copies: 2) and the page closed and opened again draw it with no further request to the server, which marks it no-store; the failed URL isn't asked for again at once either. The Plugin Catalog's Image page draws a data:image picture filled (covering its 64-point square, cropped), fitted (letterboxed inside it), clipped to a circle and with rounded corners, shows the failing URL's placeholder symbol, and keeps its unlabeled Image out of accessibility. `plugin render` reports the plugin's Image nodes and their props (url, size, width and height, circle, cornerRadius, contentMode, placeholder, label) without loading any picture, the added copy is one commit that creates one Image and changes the readout, and the catalog page renders without errors. An Image url that isn't an absolute https, http, file or data:image URL (ftp, a relative path, a data URL of text, an https URL with no host), a missing url, a mistyped size, circle or contentMode, a child, or an event is reported in errors with exit 1, naming the prop and what is wrong.

Debug ▸ Highlight Native Atoms outlines every atom view without moving it, so UI built from plugin atoms reads apart from plain SwiftUI. `plugin render` reports the container atoms (Stack, Panel, Card, Scroll, Disclosure, Overlay, Popover, Modal, Page, SidePanel), every one of them a known atom, and every other atom is a leaf. With the item off no atom carries an outline; turned on, the board's task card is outlined live, its Card as a container and its Text as a leaf, at the same frame as with it off, and the Plugin Catalog outlines each atom type it renders, including Spacer, Card and PillPicker, as a container or a leaf to match, the Card and the PillPicker keep the same frames as with it off, and hovering a Text atom shows a label naming its type that goes away when the pointer leaves. The setting persists: after a relaunch the reopened catalog is still outlined, and turning the item off removes every outline.

A task whose conversation hasn't started is scheduled once (the composer's schedule hint, or schedule set --once); scheduling saves the prompt as the schedule's own payload without starting a turn, keeps the task in Backlog with a clock badge, and lists it in schedule list. A task with its own title keeps it, while an untitled task scheduled once (from the composer or schedule set) shows Generating title… and is then named from its prompt by the provider's title turn, as a first send would, without starting a conversation turn. Removing the schedule in the hint before Send turns the clock button off and returns Send to sending. A time in the past or a blank prompt is rejected with invalid_argument. A tick before the time does nothing; a tick 30 minutes after it, inside the one-hour grace period, sends the scheduled prompt to the provider, clears the schedule, and the task follows the ordinary board lifecycle. A second tick doesn't run it again. An existing conversation still shows scheduling, offers one-time messages only, preserves its lifecycle state, keeps the scheduled message in the composer as its unsent draft while Send returns to sending, and sends the due message, including edits made to that draft since it was scheduled, to that same task and conversation, preserving its Claude session or Codex thread identifier; once it is sent, the draft is cleared from storage and from the open composer. The app bundle carries the scheduler LaunchAgent (<bundle-id>.scheduler.plist running playhouse-cli schedule tick every 60 seconds), and a plain tick on the real clock fires a schedule that has come due.

A scheduled run more than one hour late is not started. A one-time task lands in Blocked with a 'Missed scheduled run' message and its prompt kept as an unsent draft, and sending that draft starts it. A recurring schedule ticked a week late creates exactly one Blocked run task linked to its schedule, skips the older missed occurrences, and moves its next run into the future. A due run whose provider can't start lands in Blocked saying the scheduled run couldn't start, with its prompt kept as the draft.

A recurring schedule needs a title, and a weekday when it repeats weekly; once confirmed, its template is absent from the board and task list but listed by schedule list and in the Scheduled Tasks popover. A due tick creates a new board task with the schedule's title and context folders, linked by scheduleSourceTaskID, sends the prompt, records the run on the template and advances its next run by one day. A paused schedule doesn't fire, Run now starts a run immediately, and clearing the schedule turns the template into an ordinary Backlog task. A run saves no pull request mode of its own: it takes the one the pull-request-mode plugin keeps for its schedule (a Manual schedule's run reaches Review in Manual mode), and once that is changed to PR a later run reaches Review in PR mode. Saving PR for the tasks saved while PR was the default (once, at a first launch since Manual became the default) leaves such a run with no mode of its own, still inheriting its schedule's, while a run whose schedule was deleted gets PR saved as its own. The template's last run is the latest run, and the Scheduled Tasks popover's Open Last Run closes the popover and opens that run, so going back from it returns to the board.

The Scheduled Tasks sidebar button opens the Scheduled Tasks popover beside it, over the board, whose New Task (header, or the button in the empty popover) closes the popover and opens a task conversation with the schedule hint already open on Recurring; opening a scheduled task from it closes it too, so going back returns to the bare board. Opening a scheduled task shows its confirmed prompt with the schedule button on and Send in schedule mode, and its hint shows the saved repeat, day and time; changing its title and repeat in the hint and confirming with Send persists across fresh CLI reads, keeps the time, and starts no turn. Deleting a schedule removes it from schedule list and from the popover. Done in the hint of a task that is already scheduled once saves the moved time at once, without Send, keeping its prompt, Backlog state and Send's schedule mode, starting no turn, and the hint reopens on that time; schedule set without --prompt likewise moves a scheduled task while keeping its prompt and mode, and still rejects a task with no schedule with invalid_argument. Remove in the hint clears a saved schedule as well, turning the clock off and keeping the prompt in the composer, and schedule set rejects --mode, --model or --image without --prompt with invalid_argument. An existing conversation's scheduled message is moved the same way, keeping its prompt, the composer draft and the task's Review state; after it is scheduled, and after the conversation is reopened, the message stays in the composer as its draft and Send sends again while the clock stays on and the hint shows the saved time. Clearing an existing conversation's scheduled message sends nothing; in the hint, Remove leaves the message in the composer, and a composer draft already there is kept. Sending a one-time scheduled task by hand ends its schedule, so a later tick sends nothing more; a recurring template rejects a send with invalid_transition; and clearing a schedule keeps its prompt as the task's draft.

The Plugin Catalog's Card page gives a Card with no padding prop its 14-point default, while `padding: 0` removes it. `plugin render --page Card` omits the default common padding but keeps the explicit zero override on the second Card, and in the UI two otherwise identical cards have the same width while the default-padded card is 28 points taller; each card keeps its own content inside the surface.

A Claude compaction is one conversation row. A provider auto-compaction whose start Claude Code reports twice under different ids before its boundary leaves exactly one completed compaction row in the latest turn's history, with no row still in progress. A compaction that starts before the daemon is killed and ends after it, so its boundary reaches a daemon that never saw the row reported for its start, shows one in-progress row while the turn runs, before and after the restart, then one completed row with its context sizes as soon as the boundary arrives while the turn is still running, and records one compaction event. A long turn that compacts twice shows each compaction where it happened: the first after the text and tool call written before it and before the summary message Claude Code continues from, the second between the messages written after the first and its own summary, never stacked after the turn's last message. Compaction rows stored without the message they follow are placed the same way, by when each compaction finished.

A Claude Code synthetic notice longer than the automatic message preview stays whole: the streamed steered message and fresh CLI/XPC history carry every line of it under the Claude Code notice marker, between the turn's answer and Claude's reply, and a short notice is recorded unchanged too. In the transcript the long notice renders as an automatic message from Claude Code collapsed to an eight-line preview ending in an ellipsis, with a Show more control whose accessibility label names expanding the automatic message; expanding the streamed notice while its turn still runs reveals all of its text and survives the reload that gives it its history id and the reload after a later turn, and collapsing restores the preview. A short notice shows in full with no control or preview, the user's own prompts never get one, the bubble's accessibility label keeps the full text, and reopening the task shows the long notice collapsed again. The preview is Playhouse-owned presentation shared by every automatic message whatever the provider, and only Claude Code injects a synthetic message inside a turn, so Claude is the representative provider.

A Stop that arrives while Codex is still starting the thread moves the task out of In Progress at once, before Codex answers. Nothing of the message is sent: the send ends with turn_stopped, no turn starts, the prompt returns to the draft with no failure reason, and the task returns to the status it had before the send. A steer sent for that message before the Stop is stopped with it: it ends with turn_stopped, is not queued and never runs as a turn of its own. A follow-up queued during that launch stays in the queue, marked as needing the user's action, and does not run. A Stop that arrives after turn/start was sent but before Codex acknowledged the turn also leaves In Progress at once, and Codex's turn/interrupt follows as soon as the turn has its ID, leaving the task in Waiting Response. In the window Stop is enabled as soon as the message is sent, and clicking it replaces Stop at once while the provider is still held; the stopped steer's bubble leaves the transcript and its text returns to the composer with the stopped message, without an error.

A Stop that arrives while Claude Code is still starting the session moves the task to Waiting Response at once, before the session answers. The control interrupt follows as soon as the turn has started, the send settles as stopped without a failure reason, and the task stays in Waiting Response. In the window Stop is enabled as soon as the message is sent, and clicking it replaces Stop with Continue at once while the session is still starting.

A message sent while the task's earlier turn is still being stopped waits for that turn, and a Stop that arrives while it waits stops it too. That Stop answers at once without asking Codex to interrupt a second time; once the earlier turn is over the waiting send ends with turn_stopped, no second turn starts, and the task stays in Waiting Response with no failure reason. In the window Continue replaces Stop at once, the stopped Continue's message leaves the transcript without an error, and Continue stays available for the turn that was stopped first. The stopped message is saved neither as a draft nor as a prompt still being sent.

A steer sent while Codex is still starting the thread waits for the turn instead of missing it: once the turn has its ID the steer reaches that turn through turn/steer and is not queued for a turn of its own. A follow-up can be queued during the same launch, before Codex has named the conversation; steered, it reaches that turn the same way and leaves the queue. One left in the queue runs once as a turn of its own after that turn ends. In the window the steer's bubble joins the transcript and the composer clears at once, a follow-up typed with Return joins the queue at once without an error, and its row gives way to its bubble at once when steered, while Codex is still held and has not received either.

A steer sent while Claude Code is still starting the session waits for the turn instead of missing it: once the turn has started the steer reaches it as a next-priority message, the turn answers it, and it is not queued for a turn of its own. The steer is recorded inside the turn it steered, before any reply in it. In the window the steer's bubble joins the transcript and the composer clears at once, while the session is still starting and has not received it, and the turn's work stays above the bubble while it waits, while Claude Code holds it unanswered, and after its answer renders below it.

A reader that asks history to defer images (--defer-images, as the app does) gets image data only for the newest turn the user started: earlier messages with images come back marked imagesDeferred with no image data, on the newest page, on an earlier --before page, where every image waits, and in the history a send returns, while plain history stays complete and never carries the mark, and the mark is never stored. conversation images returns the exact stored images of the named messages and nothing for a message without images; in a Codex conversation, whose user images Playhouse stores the same way, an earlier image is deferred the same way and read back from the store. Naming no message fails with invalid_argument and an unknown task fails with not_found. Reopening the conversation in the visible UI reads no image data until the reader scrolls up: each earlier image then loads when its message comes into view and is shown, and a turn sent afterwards from the composer keeps the loaded images without reading them again.

A plugin installed at the taskItem placement (inline or as a button) is valid and runs with its card's task as `props.task`. Playhouse.on delivers app events to a plugin's listeners: task.statusChanged with {taskID, from, to} when its task moves between columns, app.focus when the app comes to the front, and plugin.stateChanged with {pluginID, key, value} when a saved value changes; `plugin render --event @<name>[:json]` reports how many listeners heard each, and the function Playhouse.on returns stops listening. Playhouse.throttle(fn, seconds) runs the first call at once and collapses the calls made within its cooldown into one trailing call with the latest arguments when the cooldown ends. `plugin event <name> [--payload <json>]` hands an app event to the built-in plugins' services; an unknown name is invalid_argument and a payload that is not a JSON object is a usage error. In the window, an installed task card plugin renders on every card, a Backlog card included (which has no built-in pull request controls yet), in the bottom row beside the built-in mode pill once the task has started, shows its task's status, hears the task move to Review and probes through its throttle, and probes through it again when the app comes back to the front (the window's app.focus), repeated focuses within its cooldown collapsing into at most two probes; a task card plugin with a button opens a popover showing its card's task. Only a task card's plugin may call ui.moveTask (which moves its task as dragging the card does), ui.resolveConflicts (which in the window opens its task and sends the conflict instruction) and ui.alert (which shows the board's alert); from the conversation sidebar or the board's sidebar they are unavailable, and so is the composer from a task card, the same in `plugin render`, which records each call in hostCalls, and in the window. The Plugins menu lists the card's built-ins, and disabling the built-in Pull request mode removes the card's mode pill while installed task card plugins stay, until it is enabled again. A turn's move of its task, on Codex and on Claude, is published to the services from the provider's own callbacks, and no move is dropped.

A tool call whose command is long keeps its whole command: the streamed activity and fresh CLI/XPC history carry its title as Running followed by every line of a heredoc or every character of a long single-line command, and a short command's title is recorded unchanged. While the heredoc still runs, its live command row shows only the title's first line ending in an ellipsis, with no expand control. In the transcript's Worked for list a long title shows its first line, cut to 160 characters and ending in an ellipsis, with an expand control whose accessibility label names expanding the activity title; expanding reveals all of the command and collapsing restores the preview, while the row's accessibility label keeps the full title. A short command's row shows its whole title with no control, and reopening the task shows the long title collapsed again. The preview is Playhouse-owned presentation in the activity row both providers share, and both build a command's title as Running followed by the whole command, so Claude is the representative provider.

The board sidebar's bottom is the mainSidebarBottom placement, whose plugins always use the section presentation: a manifest or an authoring request with any other presentation there, or with section anywhere else, is invalid with an error naming the rule. A section plugin gets `props.agents` with the last-known agent usage report (the same providers `usage get` reports, each with whether its CLI is installed) and `runningTasks`, each provider's count of In Progress tasks, which counts a running Codex turn. The app.launched event reaches a plugin once per launch, and the first listener a plugin adds after it was emitted still hears it once; a later listener does not. ui.confirm and ui.openURL are host calls: confirm is answered only by the board (unavailable at the conversation sidebar; in `plugin render` it resolves null), and openURL accepts only http and https URLs (anything else is invalid_argument). In the window, sections stack at the bottom of the sidebar, each under a collapsible header with the plugin's name, open by default: collapsed, they sit one above the other at the bottom, and expanding the lower one grows it upward and pushes the upper one up. A section's collapsed state is its plugin state `collapsed` and survives a relaunch. The section's plugin hears app.launched, reads both providers' running counts, gets true from ui.confirm when the user confirms the board's dialog (showing its title, message and confirm button) and false when they cancel, opens http URLs and is refused other URLs, and the built-in Agents info section is not shown when no agent CLI is installed. Authoring a plugin there starts it as a section without asking how it opens: `plugin author --placement mainSidebarBottom` with a name and the section presentation records both and the placement, and in the window Add Plugin mode shows an Add here button below the sections whose setup goes from the name straight to the editor, which says it opens as a collapsible section.

A plugin at the board's mainSidebar placement gets `props.schedules`: `tasks`, the scheduled tasks exactly as `schedule list` returns them (soonest first, each with its schedule's kind and paused state), and `needsLoginItemsApproval`; with no schedules the list is empty, and a conversation sidebar plugin gets no schedules. ui.newTask (with schedule "recurring", "once" or none) and ui.openLoginItems are host calls only the board answers: a conversation sidebar plugin is refused as unavailable, and any other schedule is invalid_argument. The board's Scheduled Tasks button and popover are the built-in scheduled-tasks popover plugin, which can't be rendered headlessly (invalid_argument). In the window, a mainSidebar page plugin lists the schedules and follows them live as one is paused, and its ui.newTask opens a new task with the schedule picker up; disabling the built-in Scheduled Tasks removes its sidebar button, and enabling it brings back the button, which opens the Scheduled Tasks popover.

The composer's / commands come from the built-in Built-in Commands headless plugin, which reads everything it shows through bridge commands and acts through ui calls. Typing / where a word starts anywhere in the composer opens a command menu listing /mcp, /plan, /goal, /skill, /login and /plugin in that order, narrowed to the commands whose name starts with what follows the /. On a Claude task /goal can't be chosen and says goal mode isn't supported by Claude, while on a Codex task it can. Choosing /plan turns plan mode on and choosing /goal on a Codex task opens the goal entry, each removing the typed command from the draft. The command menu shares the mention menu's look: the same floating panel, as wide as the mention menu, with the same section headers and highlighted-row surface. Typing a command with its own list in full lists its items, narrowed by text after a space: /mcp lists the MCP servers the composer can mention, and asked with sign-in status marks each server with the agents that need a sign-in to it (shown as a Sign in button per agent on its row); /skill lists the mentionable skills, editable ones with a working gear and built-in ones with a disabled gear; choosing either mentions it as @handle in place of the command. /login lists both agents, the task's own first, and choosing one starts that agent's sign-in, opening the link Codex's sign-in returns. /plugin lists Create Plugin first, which turns on Add Plugin mode, then the user's own plugins (never built-in ones), disabled ones marked so, each with edit, which opens the plugin's editor conversation, delete, which asks first, and a settings gear that stays disabled until plugins have settings. In the window an MCP server's gear opens the MCP page with that server's editor, its Sign in button opens the MCP page filtered to it and starts that agent's sign-in, and every choice removes the typed command. slash-commands run runs a command, chooses one of its items or presses an item's button the same way the window does and reports the plugin's host calls. Disabling the Built-in Commands plugin removes its commands from the menu and from slash-commands, and enabling it restores them. Listing without a task is a usage error and for an unknown task is not_found; running without a command, with an item for a command without a list, without an item for a command with a list, or with a button but no item is a usage error, and an unknown command, item or button is not_found.

An installed plugin whose presentation is headless and whose placement is composerActions has no button or surface, only the / commands its manifest's commands declare and its script registers with Playhouse.commands.register. They are listed after the built-in commands with the plugin's id, its icon for a command without one, and the composer and slash-commands run them alike with the composer's context: a command without a list runs at once and the text it returns replaces the typed command; a command with a list shows the items its list handler builds from bridge commands, narrowed by the typed filter, which also matches an item's keywords, choosing an item inserts the text its choose handler returns, and an item's button calls the press handler, whose host calls are reported; a command whose available handler says it can't run is listed disabled with its reason and can't be run. A command whose handler throws fails with its message, which the window shows under the composer after removing the typed command, and a plugin whose available handler fails lists its commands disabled with the error as the reason. A disabled plugin's commands aren't offered. A headless plugin without commands or at another placement, a command named like a built-in one, and a declared command its script never registers each make the plugin invalid, and an invalid plugin offers no commands.

The standalone chat's pages can be read one at a time: `conversation history --page <page-id> --limit N` returns the window that starts at that page's first message, with earlierMessageCount and laterMessageCount telling how much of the chat lies before and after it, and `--after <message-id>` continues the window forward, so jumping to an old page reads only that page's window rather than every page around it. The windows match the same slices of the full history; an unknown page or message is not_found, combining --before, --after and --page is invalid_argument, and --page on a board task is invalid_argument. In the chat, a compact column of page labels left of the transcript, centered on its height, lists the pages by title (long titles truncated), newest at the bottom, well apart, at most 10 in view at a time with no scroll bar, reading only the 10 newest labels at first and older ones, 10 at a time, only as the column is scrolled up, and shown as soon as the chat opens without waiting for the provider's model list, with the store's pages indexed by chat and age so reading the newest few never sorts the whole chat; clicking a label shows that page from its first message with only its window loaded (the transcript reports Showing earlier), scrolling down loads the following messages, the label of the page at the top of the transcript is marked current, and Latest returns to the newest messages, as does the Jump to bottom arrow centered below the labels, from an earlier page or after scrolling up the newest messages, at once and without the labels moving off the transcript's middle. Unlocked, which is the default, the labels are folded into a long thin handle at the transcript's leading edge halfway down it, and the messages keep their width: hovering the handle slides the labels out and pushes the messages right without narrowing them, widening the chat sidebar by the labels' room, which pushes the board's columns right, instead of reflowing the messages' text, they stay out as the pointer moves from the handle onto them, and moving the pointer off them folds them back in, once, even when the pointer rests beside them where the folding labels pass. The handle stays beside the open labels, thicker, under a small open lock icon that is absent while they are folded, and clicking it locks them open after the pointer leaves, closing the lock while the handle keeps its color, which persists across a relaunch; clicking it again unlocks them, opening the lock, so they fold back into the handle when the pointer leaves; agent replies end at the same right edge as the user's messages. A page separator's Recall button, with a hint that it references that conversation, returns to the bottom of the chat and shows Recalling <title> in the composer; the next message carries that page into the turn through the provider-neutral context-page seeding (the CLI's --context-page), and the indication can be removed and clears after sending. Page windows, labels and recall are Playhouse-owned and shared by Claude and Codex, so one representative provider (Claude) covers the case.

Playhouse stores every conversation turn in its own transcript store, for Codex and Claude alike. After a Codex turn and, following a provider switch, a Claude turn, a fresh daemon serves the same messages, roles, texts, providers and order without asking Codex for its thread history: Codex replies stay labeled Codex with the model that wrote them, Claude replies stay labeled Claude, and a limited read returns only the latest page with the count of earlier messages and keeps the Codex-to-Claude boundary after the last Codex message.

`task repository add-worktree` gives a task another worktree of a repository it already has, created at once on its own new branch (the given name, or a fresh one from the task title), and adding an already attached repository again does the same, so one repository can hold several worktrees, each listed with its own path and branch and persisted across fresh reads. A second worktree on a branch the task already uses is rejected and leaves the task unchanged. While a repository has several worktrees, `--repo` alone no longer picks one: remove, renew, edit and pr link fail with an error naming each worktree path and asking for `--worktree`, and `--worktree <path>`, like that worktree's chip remove badge, removes just that worktree and its folder. Each worktree's chip opens that worktree's settings. The next agent turn lists every worktree mapping and is told to open pull requests with task pr create or register them with task pr link, never to switch a worktree's branch, and to use add-worktree for another branch. `task create` can list a repository more than once: each entry is its own pending worktree with its own chip, the further automatic ones waiting as auto 2, auto 3 and so on, so each can be edited or removed on its own (with `--worktree-branch` naming it on the CLI), and starting the task gives each its own branch; giving two of them the same branch is rejected as invalid_argument and creates no task.

A pull request status read looks up the pull request GitHub has for each started worktree's checked-out branch, so one opened outside Playhouse (for example with gh pr create) is recorded with its number and URL and listed by `task get` and `task pr status` with the worktree it belongs to. Two worktrees of one repository each get their own. When a worktree's branch was switched by hand, the read records the branch actually checked out, keeps the earlier pull request listed with the task's past pull requests, and finds the new branch's pull request; a closed pull request is recorded as closed, and `task pr status` lists it with closed health beside the open one and the earlier one marked past; a later one for that branch replaces it. After one worktree's pull request merges, `task repository renew --worktree <path>` gives just that worktree a fresh branch, lists the merged pull request once with the past ones, and leaves the other worktree and its pull request as they were. A read that finds nothing leaves the task unchanged, and a Done task is never probed: its status read lists only its recorded pull requests.

`task pr link <task-id> --worktree <path> --url <pr-url>` reads the pull request from GitHub and records it on that worktree when its head branch is the worktree's checked-out branch, so `task get` and `task pr status` list it. A pull request for another branch is rejected with an error naming both branches, an invalid URL and a pull request GitHub can't find are rejected, and each failure leaves the task unchanged. With one worktree of the repository `--repo` selects it; a pull request GitHub later closes is recorded as closed on the next read, and the worktree's chip settings in the task header show it as #N · closed, linking to it; linking again replaces the link and keeps the earlier pull request listed with the task's past pull requests. A worktree switched by hand to a branch that can't be a task branch (the repository's default branch) keeps its recorded branch and pull request on a read, and linking that branch's pull request is rejected. Linking is rejected on a Done task.

Above the standalone chat's page labels, a small search field narrows them to the pages whose titles contain its text, read from the whole chat rather than only the newest ten labels, matching case-insensitively and literally: `chat page list --title <text>` returns those pages newest first, its --limit counting matches, surrounding spaces ignored, message text not searched, % and _ matching only themselves, no match an empty list, blank text the same as no filter, and --title without a value invalid_argument. In the chat, the field sits just above the labels the handle slides out, inside their hovered area; typing filters the labels, including a page older than the labels first read, and clicking a match jumps to that page; while the field has the keyboard, unlocked labels stay out after the pointer leaves them. Text that matches nothing shows No matching pages, and the clear button, or Escape, restores every label. The search is Playhouse-owned and shared by Claude and Codex, so one representative provider (Claude) covers the case.

A standalone chat shows what each turn cost under the turn's last reply. Providers report usage once per turn, so a history read marks only the last assistant reply of each turn with that turn's recorded usage (input, output, cache read and cache write exactly as the turn's Token Stats row), leaving the user's message and earlier commentary unmarked, and an empty chat has nothing marked. A second turn that replies twice (Claude Code's no-visible-output notice between its answer and a later reply) marks only its last reply, with its own row, while the first reply keeps the first turn's. A history page that ends inside a turn marks none of that turn's messages, because its last reply is on a later page, while an earlier turn whose reply is in the page stays marked, including a reply that ends the page when the next page starts another turn. In the chat, the marked reply shows a small token counter (1.6K tokens) directly beneath it, whose tooltip names the turn's total and its four buckets, while prompts and a turn's earlier replies show none, and clicking it opens the window's usual Token Stats modal for the chat with the turn rows, which Done closes. Usage is attributed to Playhouse's local turn on the shared recording path for both Claude and Codex, so one representative provider (Claude) covers the case.

A provider divider and a goal achievement stay right after the message they were recorded after. A long Claude history whose switch from Codex sits on its older page, with a switch to Claude and back that sent nothing stored on the same message, has one Codex-to-Claude divider after the last Codex message in complete and paged CLI/XPC history, the empty switch pair dropped, and the newest page leaves that message out; another turn leaves the divider where it was. Opened on its newest page, the visible transcript draws neither that divider nor a goal achievement recorded after the last Codex message, at the bottom or anywhere after a newer message, and they stay hidden after a new message is sent from the composer; a goal achievement recorded after the latest turn's folded commentary follows that turn's question, above its answer, not the newest message. Scrolling up loads the older page and shows the one divider, then that goal achievement, right after the last Codex message and before the next question, with no Switched to Codex divider. The placement is Playhouse-owned and the same for both providers, so one switch from Codex to Claude covers the case.

A development build reports the development phase and refuses to check, download or install, and its Check for Updates menu item is disabled, so it never updates itself. A stable build checks the signed release feed: before a check it is up to date with no offer; a check offers the newer release with its version, release date and notes, shown as a compact Update button at the trailing end of the window's title bar whose tooltip names them, which a fresh read still reports, and finds it through the release's asset list (GitHub's latest-release API) when the feed link fails; the daily automatic check does not reach the feed again within a day, even when the feed is gone, while a manual check from the app menu then reports the failure; and turning daily checks off is saved and makes an automatic check a no-op. A newer release built for another architecture or needing a newer macOS is not offered. An app in a folder it can't write to says to move Playhouse to Applications, refuses to check, and doesn't offer even a release it already found, so no update button shows.

A release whose manifest is signed by another key is refused at check time, so nothing is offered and the failure is shown with the signature reason. A release whose archive grew after signing is offered but refused at download for its size, and one with a changed byte of the same size is refused for its checksum: each time nothing is staged beside the installed app, the failure is shown with its reason, installing reports there is nothing ready, and the installed app is untouched.

Downloading a checked release from a feed served over HTTP reports its progress while it runs, rising to the whole archive, and a second download meanwhile is refused as busy. Canceling stops it, keeps the release offered without a failure, and leaves nothing staged or half-downloaded; canceling with no download running is refused. A check when the feed is gone is reported as unreachable and shown as a failed update that keeps the release offered. Retrying once the feed is back downloads and stages the release with progress rising to the whole archive, and a half-written message then holds the restart: it waits to restart into the staged release while the installed app stays the old version.

Downloading a checked release reports progress and stages it beside the installed app, ready to restart. Installing swaps the whole bundle in place, so the app, its command-line tool and its bridge daemon are the new version; the running daemon is stopped and the next request starts a new one; the staged and previous copies are cleaned up; the app is told it was updated, with the release notes, until the notice is opened, which saves it as seen, or a day has passed; the offer is gone, and checking the same feed again reports it up to date.

A release whose bridge daemon doesn't run passes download verification but fails the installer's health check after the swap, so the installer puts the previous version back: the installed app, command-line tool and daemon are the old version again, nothing is left staged, and the app is told that the update didn't install and why until that is dismissed, while the release stays offered. A release whose command-line tool doesn't run can't start its own installer, so the install is reported as failed until dismissed and the installed app is untouched.

While an agent is running a turn and a message typed in another task is unsent, installing a downloaded release once agents are idle doesn't start the installer: it reports one running agent and one message being written, the update is saved as waiting with Restart to update and a tooltip giving both reasons, and the installed app stays the old version. A task's unsent description that was never typed in the composer doesn't hold it. When the turn finishes the half-written message still holds the install; once it is cleared, the daemon installs the release by itself without another request, the turn's answer is kept once, and the installed app and its command-line tool are the new version.

The installed app's own command-line tool accepts its bundle with verify-bundle and refuses a copy changed after signing. Updating the app a request comes from, with no test target, stops that app's own bridge daemon on its private service and installs over it, so the app, its command-line tool and the next daemon on that service report the new version; a daemon another service started from the old bundle reports that it was replaced on disk and is retired by the next request, which starts one from the new bundle (the visible suite's sandboxed runner can't start a daemon itself, so only the headless suite starts one on another service). With the app's window running, the installer asks it to quit, the app quits by itself rather than being stopped, and the installer reopens the new version in the same data folder and bridge service, where it says it was updated; the headless suite runs no window, so nothing is reopened.

Restarting to update while a Claude Code turn is running doesn't wait for it: with the update waiting for the agent, installing now starts the installer, a second install while it runs is refused as busy, and the installer stops the app's own bridge daemon and installs over it; with the window running, the app quits by itself when the installer asks rather than being stopped. The send that was waiting on the stopped daemon fails as unavailable, the Claude Code process keeps running, the next daemon is the new version and reattaches the same run; when that daemon is stopped in turn, it refuses new requests as exiting instead of dropping them and logs each one, gives up its socket before it exits so callers already queued on it are refused rather than dropped, and the daemon that follows starts only once it has exited, the CLI and the window's update check send them again to the daemon that follows (the headless suite runs no window, so only the CLI's are sent), and that daemon takes the same run back; and when the turn finishes its answer is kept once and the task settles through its outcome.

Restarting to update while a Codex turn is running doesn't wait for it: with the update waiting for the agent, installing now starts the installer, a second install while it runs is refused as busy, and the installer stops the app's own bridge daemon and installs over it; with the window running, the app quits by itself when the installer asks rather than being stopped. The send that was waiting on the stopped daemon fails as unavailable, the shared Codex app-server keeps running, the next daemon is the new version and reconnects to the same server; when that daemon is stopped in turn, it refuses new requests as exiting instead of dropping them and logs each one, gives up its socket before it exits so callers already queued on it are refused rather than dropped, and the daemon that follows starts only once it has exited, the CLI and the window's update check send them again to the daemon that follows (the headless suite runs no window, so only the CLI's are sent), and that daemon takes the same server back; and when the turn finishes its answer is kept once and the task settles through its outcome.

The CLI's help is printed from its single command catalog, which the parser also requires: help, help <group> and <group> --help print that group's declared commands with their usage and a one-line description, and --for <audience> narrows them to one agent. The standalone chat's help lists the board commands, task create and every schedule command but no internal command (schedule tick) and no task-only command (task outcome, task progress publish, task pr autopilot, task move to Done --discard-changes); the task agent's help lists those task commands and still no internal one; the side chat's help lists only the read-only board commands its hook lets it run, the same list it is refused with, and never the option that starts a task; the plugin editor's help lists plugin render and no task or schedule command. The full help lists everything, internal commands marked. An unknown group or audience and an undeclared command or operation are refused as invalid_argument, pointing at help. Following the chat's help, a new task is created and scheduled once for tomorrow at 09:00 with schedule set, and it is in schedule list and in the Scheduled Tasks popover with that run time. The help reads only the CLI's own catalog and the schedule goes through the shared board manager, so provider selection cannot change either; no provider runs.
